utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. The sitting is now resumed. We should first announce that for technical reasons, it has not been possible to give effect yesterday afternoon to the redaction proposal. I don't understand too well the technicalities involved, but the way it looks to me is this: that you have a 30-minute interval in which to make the redaction, and after that the only redaction possible is that the offending paragraphs or passages will be redacted for further outward transmission, and that will be done this morning. Okay. So now we give the floor to counsel for Mr. Kvocka. That is to say, to Counsel Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am going to use my hour and a half by focusing on the most important questions which are dealt with in detail, otherwise, both in the appellant's brief as well as later on in response to the Prosecutor. As the Presiding Judge noted yesterday, the Trial Chamber condemned Kvocka for persecution, killings and torture, accountable according to Article 5(3) of the Statute of the International Tribunal against persons listed in the confidential annex to the indictment. The Trial Chamber rules that the basis for Kvocka's liability and responsibility was as co-perpetrator in a joint criminal enterprise, and in that regard, in its judgement it underlined at that Mr. Kvocka did not personally take part in a single criminal act or, rather, in any act which would lead to a criminal act being committed for which he was charged and for which he was pronounced guilty. I should also like to state at the outset that my colleague took the floor yesterday, Mr. Fila and Mr. Jovan Simic, and they dealt with certain questions. They raised certain issues, and Mr. Fila said that -- announced that I would be speaking on other matters today here before you. Regardless of how this has been put forward, certain grounds in the appellant's brief are appellant's brief boils down to two basic grounds for appeal and that is that the Trial Chamber in bringing in its judgement erred in the facts. That is the first point. And second, that the Trial Chamber also made legal errors in finding my client guilty on the counts relevant to that. We therefore consider, Your Honours, that these errors fulfil the standard which are provided for by Article 25 of the Statute of the International Tribunal and also the standards which were established to a certain extent through the practice of this Tribunal in trials held and proceedings held here so far. Of course, we shall speak at greater length on that matter in due course. I should now like to look at the standards required for Article 25 of the Statute. When we come to the matter of legal errors, we support the decision made in the Furundzija case, and on that occasion let me just remind you briefly that the Trial Chamber -- or, rather, the Appeals Chamber -- in that case found that the Appeals Chambers as the supreme interpreters of law before this International Tribunal can, by virtue of their official duty, put right certain errors of law which occur in first-instance judgements. Of course, this implies and understands that the errors are of such intensity that they led to a miscarriage of justice and an erroneous finding of guilty. When we deal with factual errors, errors of facts in establishing the facts, that is a slightly more delicate and sensitive question and slightly more complex as well. This question was broached yesterday by Mr. Fila, but I don't think Mr. Fila rounded off what he wished to say and elaborated this very complex question as fully as he could have done. A "reasonable judgement" was the term used, and I think that the standard for reasonable judgement is just a synonym which is a guideline telling the Appeals Chamber how it should assess and weigh up the findings of the Trial Chamber with respect to facts. Let me say in this context that the Appeals Chamber in the Kupreskic case also dealt with this question, and on that occasion it concluded the following, and I am going to quote. The Appeals Chamber on that occasion found the following, and I quote: "The function of this International Tribunal is to decide upon the guilt or innocence of individuals in keeping with the standards of procedure and evidence which were followed by all the civilised countries of the world." The second principle which was stressed, in order to show the full complexity of the subject matter, is also something that the Trial Chamber affirmed or Appeal Chamber affirmed through a conclusion that reads as follows: "The Tribunal does its best to follow the principle established by the first prosecutor at Nuremberg, that the events must be borne out by reasonable proof and evidence"; which means that Kvocka and his Defence team sees the notion of the standard of reasonable as a synonym and that it should be viewed through the highest achievements of modern law as we know it and as the legal systems of the world know it. And that is why my colleague Mr. Fila should not feel that Judges passing that type of judgement are not reasonable. In another finding of the Appeals Chamber, I think it was in the Tadic trial, the Tadic case, the Trial Chamber or Appeals Chamber concluded among other things, and I'm quoting: "It is essential to say that two Judges acting in a reasonable way can very easily reach different conclusions on the basis of the same evidence put before them." Therefore, we consider that it is not a matter of whether the Appeals Chamber is looking into the objections reasonably, errors of fact, errors in weighing up the evidence and without violating any person's reasonable characteristics can bring in the wrong conclusion. We must bear in mind that Judges are men and women and that men and women can see things in different ways. One person can see a thing in a different way than another, but there is hierarchy here and that is authority, the authority of the final Appeals Chamber, the second instance of the Appeals Chamber whose -- who has greater weight. That is why we consider that Mr. Kvocka's appeal and the matters it has set forth satisfies those standards and that the Appeals Chamber can fully look into them and weigh them up. We do agree with the Prosecution as well and what it says in his response, that every error of whatever kind on -- error on a question of law invalidating the decision. The Appeals Chamber must assess whether violations that are indicated and the violations of law, whether they exist indeed and what influence they had on the first instance judgement and then make their own finding and decision with respect to whether they're going to accept the grounds for appeal or reject them. We furthermore consider, and I'd like to underline this fact once again, that Kvocka meets all the standards for the Appeals Chamber to be able to accept all his grounds for appeal and make a ruling and decision acquitting him. I should now like to refer briefly to the question of the right to a fair trial. Kvocka here did not refer to that directly, but he did indicate the problem. He pointed it out. And there was a lot more mentioned about that yesterday by Mr. Jovan Simic and Mr. Fila. And it is in this direction that I should like to say a few words here and now, more for practical purposes and as a contribution for us to solve this problem. For us to be able to understand what we are talking about we must start out with what we have in our particular case. Kvocka considers that the indictment not only has the function to inform the accused of the charges being brought against him but that the indictment also has a much broader responsibility, if I can use that word. First of all, through its indictment the Prosecution itself sets him -- sets itself an indictment task, if I can put it that way. It tells the Court what it is going to prove, and that is the system of links in the general chain, and that is how Kvocka views this. And when I view it this way, too, I must take a look at what we have in this case. And if this boils down to the tasks through the indictment that the Prosecution has set itself. It has informed the Trial Chamber that it will seek to prove what it has set out in the indictment and given the Defence elements to prepare its Defence case. Now, the indictment in Kvocka's case reads as follows, and it says that Kvocka was the camp commander. Let me repeat: Camp commander is what it says. Then Kvocka is the deputy camp commander. Then he is the superior person to everyone, to all -- superior to everyone in the camp, those who come to the camp as visitors, the investigators. He was just not the superior when he was the deputy commander. He was responsible for accommodation, for the food in the camp, for the lack of medicines. He is responsible for the lack of health protection. He is responsible for the lack of water. In a word, Kvocka is the person who is absolutely responsible for everything in the camp. So that was the indictment task that the Prosecution set out to prove. It informed Kvocka, and it informed the Trial Chamber of what its task was going to be. Following that line, in its opening address, the Prosecution said Kvocka, and let me repeat this, Your Honours, on the basis of the facts or, rather, of the above-mentioned or previously mentioned fact that Kvocka is responsible both as a member of a joint criminal enterprise and all the rest, let me underline once again the Prosecution sees the notion of responsibility of Kvocka's responsibility as co-perpetrator in a joint criminal enterprise based on the Tadic judgement builds up on the elements that exist in the indictment: That Kvocka is the commander; that he was the first man in the camp; that the degree of his volition, his knowledge, et cetera, was absolutely present. And that had the Prosecution proved all these charges in the indictment, that Kvocka was the command and deputy commander, I don't think we would have to ask ourselves whether he would be responsible under the joint criminal enterprise section. But we have to go back now to what remains of the indictment task before the Trial Chamber for the Prosecution. Your Honours, absolutely nothing. The Prosecution before this Trial Chamber has managed to prove nothing of what it claims in its indictment. Kvocka was not the commander. Kvocka was not the deputy commander of the camp. Kvocka was not responsible for the hygienic conditions or health conditions or the food situation or the investigations and interrogations. Kvocka was not responsible for anything that the Prosecution claimed in its indictment which it never amended. It only looked at the existing factual premises and added the responsibility for the so-called joint criminal enterprise. Now, the question arises of what is Kvocka, who was Kvocka, what was Kvocka in the Omarska camp? And Honourable Judge asked Mr. Prcac, I think, what was Prcac in the camp. And to that question there are two answers. The first answer is the answer which was concluded by the Trial Chamber on the basis of the appellant brief. That is this, and I quote: " Kvocka was the functional dependent of the komandir of the guard service." Let me repeat: "The functional deputy of the komandir of the guard service." That was the Trial Chamber's response. Our response, our answer is quite different, and I'll elaborate that answer later on, but let's just for purposes of comparison say this. Kvocka a policeman. He was a professional policeman. He was employed in the police section, in the police station department of Omarska and he was deployed and did the work of the duty policeman in a system of extraordinary security for the camp. And I'll go into those matters later on, but I merely wanted to inform Your Honours of what Kvocka actually was in Omarska pursuant to the Trial Chamber's conclusions and what he was in our view. For us to be able to expound on the matter and the situation as to why Kvocka was and how he came to be a professional policeman on the job, on the beat at Omarska, I'll have to go back to look at the structure of that unfortunate camp of Omarska. And as my colleagues suggested, and I agree with them fully, they are in our conscience and the conscience of humanity. There is nothing I contest there. But the Omarska camp was established pursuant to a decision and order of the Crisis Staff and Simo Drljaca. Unfortunately for him, unfortunately for Kvocka and all the other people who were detained there and all the other people who worked there, it was established on the territory which territorially speaking covered by the police station and department and sector of Omarska, which is the lowest organisational form that a police station can have. It was dislocated because of the territory which could not have been covered. In the functional sense, they have absolutely no competencies or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authority at all. It was just an outlet which dealt with control, traffic control. It was not authorised to undertake investigations of any kind or even take in any criminal reports -- if anybody had had a brawl in a cafe, for example. So that was the rank of that outlet and its policemen. It was the lowest possible level. And that's where Kvocka had his own work post, and it was called the leader of the patrol sector or patrol region or whatever you like to call it. Now, what does that mean? It means that Kvocka had a region which covered just several villages and with his colleague he would patrol those vision according to a schedule. He would go into the cafes, coffee bars, meet people, and he was a sort of link between the authorities and the local population. That's what Kvocka's job was. That's what he did. And we have handed in documents to bear that out. On the 17th of June, for example -- perhaps it might have been the 21st now, I'm not sure now -- he was redeployed when the Serb police force was established. He received the same work post. He did the same job with the same working tasks. Unfortunately, on the 28th and 29th, to his unfortunate circumstances, he was the person on duty. It could have been Mladjo Radic. It could have been anyone else when in the morning hours he was informed over the telephone that as the duty officer he had to go to the compound of the Omarska mine. The order came from his komandir at the police station, the one who was his immediate superior within the frameworks of his police activities. Kvocka went there and saw that some people had been detained there. He saw that a system had been established for providing security, and his komandir informed him of the situation and says, Who are you? He says I'm the duty officer. He introduced himself. He says, Where is your commander? He says He's asleep. And of course that komandir was Zeljko Meakic. He says Wake your komandir up; tell him that you have been assigned the task of providing extraordinary security for the investigation centre set up in Omarska and this will only last for a few days. Now, before Meakic arrived, according to the rules of service, alert the reserve police force and bring them in here to provide security. That's what Kvocka did. He goes back to the police station, and through the system of police functioning, which exists in police systems all over the world, he alerts the right people, and a group of 20 men is formed which goes to Omarska. And as the duty officer, Kvocka takes them there. And then the superior takes over these individuals and deploys them to set guard jobs. Everybody had his post, and they assumed that post. And then some of the detainees who were already there, Your Honours -- according to the investigations, that has been proved -- this took place two or three days earlier, this unfortunate camp was established two or three days prior to that. Somebody could have concluded that Kvocka had some other position. He came in. He took on orders. He goes back. He alerts the people. He organises the people, he sends them back. He brings them in and turns them over to the komandir who deploys them to the guard post. To an ordinary observer, this might have seemed as if Kvocka was some sort of superior officer. No. Kvocka was simply the duty officer on that evening in the police station and happened to be doing his duties, going about his duties as was provided for by the rules of service in the public security system or the police station. And that's how the camp came to be established. Mr. Meakic didn't know that it had been established. Mr. Meakic on that particular day himself ordered Kvocka to continue his duty shift although he had been on duty all night because Mr. Meakic wanted to try to prevent the police station or the police sector to provide security. Not because he knew that this would be something that it turned out to be later on but because this was his position. He knew that with respect to the potential in the police station he wasn't able to do it himself. So he tried to do this the whole day and wasn't successful. But the camp was established nonetheless. And during our -- the production of evidence during our case, we claimed that that was not true. We presented a decision dated the 31st of May, 1992, which was signed by Mr. Drljaca in which the organisational structure of the camp was strictly provided for. Point by point it was set out, who was supposed to do what. Whose job it was to do what. Who was responsible for what. And quite simply, who reported to whom. In our desire to prove what we are claiming - and that was our duty, to prove that - and to each of those points Kvocka in particular and the other Defence counsel after that presented evidence, and the Trial Chamber accepted this, that the structure of the camp, of Omarska camp, was completely established in a way that was pursuant to Simo Drljaca's initial decision. And in that decision it explicitly states that all the duties with respect to providing security within the camp should be provided by members of the police sector or police outlet of the police station of Omarska. This is the so-called extraordinary security. It exists in the Rules of Procedure which I attached to the evidence and put it in the records of the Honourable Judges who will have the opportunity to acquaint themselves with it. And they will see how it is envisaged, this extraordinary security, who does what; who is in charge. And in one paragraph which is quoted in my submission, it says the person who ordered extraordinary security is the one in control. That was Simo Drljaca, in point 32. Is even envisages a coordinator who will coordinate all the segments and structure of extraordinary security. The Trial Chamber accepted there that the Prosecution has proven that the structure of the Omarska camp was the way it was; that is, as ordered by Simo Drljaca. So I underline this conclusion that the security of Omarska provided internal security. There were actually four types of security. First, security of the mine itself. The mines were standing in the entrance to the mine. They were also part of security. Second category, military security. There was a broader structure including Territorial Defence. They secured the perimeter of Omarska. We did not deal with this, but we did deal with this in the Stakic case where it was mined. However, this had nothing to do with our type of security. What we had here was an Intervention Platoon of Special Police. That Intervention Platoon indeed spent 10 to 15 days there in the beginning of January, and they were a cause of a lot of problems. You even have on the record evidence that Mr. Simo Drljaca was calling upon his superiors in Banja Luka to remove the Intervention Platoon because they were out of all control. They were uncontrollable even by their superiors. Without affecting accommodation, without affecting investigators, without affecting anything at all, Kvocka was simply the duty officer in this security detail. And I come back to my earlier assertion, bearing in mind that Kvocka was an active-duty policeman, that he was a duty officer, that he was keeping duty on the corner, sometimes entering an office -- and people didn't know that it was not Kvocka's own office, it was just a 18 square metre room. We have evidence of this on record -- a room which was manned by two or three typists where investigators would come to dictate records, where duty officers would sit, Radic or somebody else. And that was that notorious room which was sometimes alleged to be Kvocka's office. It was not. I allow for the possibility that under those circumstances it was perfectly understandable for someone who is not familiar with the building seeing Kvocka entering the building, not knowing about his guard post and seeing Kvocka talking to people, which was not a secret, that person could have gained the impression that Kvocka had some influence. The position of a man in extraordinary security is different from the position of a guard who simply stands guard duty for 12 hours. We believe that this we have -- in this we have provided an answer of what Kvocka's role was in Omarska camp. Let us now look at the situation in the context of events that were occurring at the time. In 1992, when the unfortunate war in Bosnia-Herzegovina began that took a toll of 200 or 300.000 people; destroyed 500, 600.000 houses; made 2 million people displaced; and had immeasurable consequences; in 1992 when this notorious came was established, in the minds of Kvocka and the other people involved, it was a temporary investigation centre resulting from the extraordinary circumstances that had arisen, and those circumstances were the armed conflicts that had already produced hundreds of dead prisoners. At the checkpoint before the events in Kozarac, the policeman from the Omarska Police Station fired at three members of the Serbian army. Judge Schomburg, in his summary, says that those were minor incidents compared to what happened later. Yes, from the viewpoint of Judge Schomburg. But from the viewpoint of the people who lived in that area where tensions were running very high, which was populated by ordinary people who were under media pressure that is difficult to fathom, the situation was completely different. For several days, you have been witness to it yourself, media pressure was raging. The reason was that an Albanian boy had drowned and a misinformation that he was chased by three Serbs into the river launched in a rage worldwide [as interpreted]. That is the scale of media frenzy that we are talking about. Now, how could you expect that a person like Kvocka could have fathomed the intent of that camp, especially after being told that it would only last for two days. And that was after all concerned. Witness B says in the first days the food was good. There was enough meat. Yes, the guards say so too. After interrogation, after questioning, you will be released. And that's indeed what happened in the first days. People were released to go to their homes. In one day, several busloads of people were released. However, things changed later. And then came the notorious order of Mr. Drljaca that no one should be released any more. However, that order was not received by the duty officer of Meakic. It was received by Josic and the people who were conducting the investigations. The Omarska camp was a punishment facility for security men as well. We have seen that every 15 hours -- every 15 minutes even in this courtroom guards are changing because this is a difficult job. In Omarska, their shifts lasted 12 hours. They believed that those were extraordinary circumstances. That was the degree of their understanding, of their imagination, of their conscience. They were kept on the same diet for a long time. In his 17 days in Omarska, Kvocka ate the same food that the prisoners got. And now Kvocka is supposed to have the intent to participate in a joint criminal enterprise where he is eating the same food as prisoners. Gentlemen for the Prosecution say it is not the same thing. He could have brought sandwiches from home. I agree it is not the same, but that is not what we are talking about. We are talking about the elements of his understanding. Kvocka and Nusret Sivac who was mentioned yesterday, they got the same rations of warm lunch. Nusret Sivac, unfortunately, got only one in 24 hours. That food was abominable. Don't misunderstand me. I don't want to justify anything. I'm just talking about the position of those people. If it is my intention to expel somebody, would I eat the same food that was qualified here as abominable? That's what I wanted to say about Omarska, the way it was established, its structure and its functioning, and now I would like to move on to the issues that relate to our appeal itself. Speaking of errors of fact, I have to emphasise that in one of our grounds we contested the conclusion of the Trial Chamber's judgement that Mr. Kvocka said in his interview to the Prosecution that Zeljko Meakic had appointed guard shift commanders. We believe that statement was used as a basis which later served to make erroneous conclusions. He was a functional replacement for the guard shift leader. We dealt in our appellate's brief with this issue at length. We must say that no method of interpretation of Mr. Kvocka's statement cannot possibly lead to the conclusion that the Trial Chamber arrived at. Kvocka, and I'm quoting, said: "Zeljko Meakic appointed some people from among the shift," and I am emphasising, "From among the shift." The Trial Chamber gave this term the meaning "shift leader." I must emphasise, Your Honours, that "shift leader" is a term that exists in normal police structure. It is a work job in regular police hierarchy in the country where I come from, just as the job of leader of patrol sector. Kvocka was shift leader. In 1994, he was appointed shift leader. So Mr. Kvocka, as an experienced policeman, a man who has graduated from the higher police school, knows very well what the duties of shift leader Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are, uses the term shift leader as he understands it. He is responsible on behalf of the group, because when he says, "I was not always aware of all the details but I would compare lists and find out who was there and who wasn't," linguistically speaking or logically speaking, there is no basis for deriving the conclusion that Kvocka was appointed shift leader. My colleagues say other evidence proved it later. It doesn't matter whether other evidence proved it later or not. I am saying that this conclusion is erroneous in itself, and it meets the standards that I spoke of earlier. Another topic related to this issue was taken up in the work of the Trial Chamber. The issue arose whether it was allowed for the interview given by Mr. Kvocka to the Prosecution be entered into evidence. Kvocka was against this. He gave me very detailed arguments for being opposed to this, but there is one of them that I consider of particular importance. Many decisions made by Trial Chambers, Appeals Chambers as well, gave primacy to a direct examination of a witness in the courtroom. That is logical and that is good. And we believed that Mr. Kvocka, who appeared as a witness in the courtroom, made himself available to the Prosecution, to the Defence, and even to the Honourable Judges to be asked any question that was of interest to them. Based on that examination, especially with regard to the Prosecution, a record ensued and a transcript. Especially one thing is important. He said to Ms. Somers, "Stop trying to put in my mouth that I said he was shift commander or shift leader, because I never said that." That is why we believe these requests should be made part of the evidence. In our case, two different standards are applied. Mr. Prcac and Mr. Radic had also given interviews to the Prosecution, but they did not testify in the courtroom. I thought that in such a situation -- and Kos as well. Kos as well. Prcac and Kos did not give -- gave interviews to the Prosecution and did not testify. I believe that in that situation, the Trial Chamber could have accepted those interviews as evidence, unlike the situation where an accused made himself available to the Judges to be examined. In this situation, we believed -- we believe that the Trial Chamber should not have accepted the interview into evidence, because it's also a violation of the principle of directness. By which standard can we arrive at the conclusion that we can trust something provided that it is told truthfully without giving a solemn oath and without any of the prerequisites for testifying before a Trial Chamber? The question arises, what is the probative value of an interview given in the offices of the Prosecution? Is it greater than the probative value of testimony given before the Trial Chamber? For all these reasons, we believe that this system was flawed and that this is another error of the Trial Chamber. Yet another error in fact is in the following: The Trial Chamber concluded, and I quote: "A great number of witnesses testified that Kvocka was in a position of authority and have convinced the Trial Chamber of this." In its judgement, the Trial Chamber demonstrates this evidence. The first group is made up of, I quote: "Evidence that include details. And a second group of evidence which are additional evidence of Kvocka's superior position in relation to guards provided by witnesses," unquote. Your Honours, Mr. Fila spoke clearly yesterday that the Trial Chamber had concluded that Kvocka, Radic, or Prcac had no position of authority which would entail elements of command responsibility or which would give them the status of superiority. As to the first group of witnesses, the Trial Chamber included Mirsad Alisic, AG, Susic, Azedin Oklopcic and Witness AI. Your Honours, I will not deal with them, name them by name, but in my appellate's brief, I mentioned them. I have, however, to stress certain things that really undermine the findings of the Trial Chamber regarding facts. The Trial Chamber conclude that Kvocka left Omarska on the 23rd of June, 1992. It was his last workday in Omarska, a workday in which Kvocka spent his time looking for an explanation for things that hurt him and things that befell him. I'm talk about this later. That same Trial Chamber concluded that Sifeta Susic was arrested and came to Omarska camp on the 24th of June. Your Honours, the witness is testifying. He testified about the acts and position of Kvocka, his conduct, but he's testifying after the fact that the Trial Chamber found that in actual fact Kvocka had left, and that standard is very dubious as a result. Mr. Kvocka did not contest that at some time, around the 27th or 28th of June when he visited Omarska because some relatives of his were detained there, too, he brought some medicines to Mrs. Susic. She was a working colleague of his. My learned colleague said we didn't cross-examine Ms. Susic. Of course we didn't because we considered it groundless to cross-examine an individual who at no point in time was there together with Kvocka in the camp for her to be able to make any conclusions about Kvocka of any kind. However, my learned friend, or rather, my learned friends of the Prosecution forget the fact that we were very rigorous in cross-examining Mrs. Sifeta Susic when she lied before this Trial Chamber about the position occupied by Mr. Kvocka before the war in Omarska when she claimed that he was the commandeer, or commander, the deputy commander, and there was a very unfortunate scene here that took place and the way in which she concluded her testimony in response to Mr. Riad's question. We then demonstrated that the witness had perhaps suffered there, perhaps this one more than others, but she had a motive. She -- because she was detained by people whom she had previously worked with for years. So Mrs. Sifeta Susic, let me repeat, worked in the police station from the very beginning until she was sent away in 1992 from that police station department for the mere reason that she was a Muslim, and I can say that quite openly here. That is true. But she was sent away by Simo Drljaca, and she was angry towards her colleagues. She felt rancour. But Mr. Kvocka did his best to find a remedy, to find some medicine that he personally didn't have. He got some from his neighbour to help the lady as one human being towards another, and that is what Mrs. Sifeta Susic did say during her testimony. And in that group there are other individuals, Kerim Mesanovic being a case in point. He was also a man who came to Omarska on the 24th of June. Mesanovic Kerim who testified that he saw Kvocka, that he saw Kvocka issuing orders to the guards. And the Trial Chamber found itself that Kvocka's effective last day in Omarska was the 22nd of June. Of course, Mr. Mesanovic couldn't have even recognised on the photo spread Mr. Kvocka. He failed to recognise him at all. But this is what troubles the whole system, this inconsistency in the judgement. You have two conclusions, two reasonable conclusions by the Trial Chamber when we speak of Kvocka once again. Witness J, for example, claims that she was arrested on the 9th, that she came to Omarska on the 9th. And the Trial Chamber accepts that as fact in order to assess Kvocka's status and position. However, that same Trial Chamber also concludes and takes as fact, at face value, that Kvocka was something there that they themselves don't know what he was, and they deduce this from the testimony of Nusret Sivac, the witness who was taken into custody and brought to Omarska for the first time on the 10th of June. And he testified; he said that witness J was arrested two or three days later, because he went to her and told her that she was likely to be arrested. So these are two facts that wipe out each other. They were arrested on the same day, Nusret Sivac, Kerim Mesanovic and Sifeta Susic. They were all arrested on that same day. Sifeta Susic, however, depicts events quite differently and quite in the opposite way to the other two. Sifeta Susic says in the middle of July he saw Kvocka in Omarska issuing orders. He tells the Trial Chamber about certain facts. Now, I myself allow for the fact that there can be certain discrepancies in recollections and so on, but you can't have somebody not being in the camp of Omarska and a witness say that, yes, he did see him, and yes, he did see him issue orders. And when he was shown a photo spread with all the different images of people, he didn't recognise Kvocka at all. So those are the facts upon which the Trial Chamber reached its conclusions. And I would like to focus on the essence of what led to the error of fact, and that is this: None of these witnesses speak of Kvocka as being the deputy commander of the guard service. Obsid [phoen] Mirsad. That's a separate case in point, and I quote -- I quoted from this passage and indicated that the Prosecutor should have been more restrictive in bringing in witnesses because a false witness who engaged in perjury is the most dangerous kind of witness in a court of law. He says, "Kvocka, on the 31st of May, said he was the commander of the camp." Now, the Trial Chamber rejected this observation that Kvocka was the camp commander. But from that rejected observation, they draw the conclusion that he was the equivalent of the deputy guard shift service. So there's no pointing of contact there, or there -- it was an even more drastic mistake. And that was the testimony by Oklopcic Azedin. The Trial Chamber concluded and said the following: The witness Oklopcic testified and said that Kvocka and Meakic were on duty shifts for 24 hours, whereas the rest did their duty shifts of 12 hours; and from that Oklopcic deduces that Kvocka had a different kind of status and a different kind of position. That's his conclusion. That's what he concludes. The Trial Chamber rejects the first premise because it incontestably asserted that they all had 12-hour shifts, without exception. But then it goes on to conclude that Kvocka's stay remained being what he was. None of these witnesses mentioned, not a single one of these witnesses ever mentioned that Kvocka was the deputy commander for security. Not a single one. Furthermore, a realistic possibility for making assessments, and we mentioned witness Nusret Sivac which is quite a separate case, the testimony of Nusret Sivac to which the Trial Chamber refers is an event that took place on the 10th of June. It did happen, and Kvocka took part in that event. In a positive way, might I say. It is true that Nusret Sivac on the 10th of June -- and we're talking about a former policeman once again -- he was taken into custody and brought to Omarska. It is true that members of the Intervention Platoon on that occasion mistreated him. That is true as well. It is also true that Kvocka, on that occasion, was the duty officer in Omarska. He happened by. He happened to witness this scene, and as a policeman and as a human being and as a person who knew Nusret Sivac -- he knows his family as well, and his sister was Kvocka's uncle's partner. They were living together -- he went up to the men -- to him to ask, "How come you're there?" Why are you here? And his answer was, "I have no idea." So Kvocka was surprised to see him there. And then Kvocka went to check all this out as the duty officer and a friend who wanted to help. He goes upstairs and he comes back and says Ranko Mijic said one of the chiefs of the investigating group, that he was erroneously taken into custody and detained, that he should be sent home. But this was an occasion when Kvocka, like at any other time, tried to help and even had the courage to go up to the Intervention Platoon chief and say, "Guys, you don't do things like that." He went to their head, their chief, and then this stopped. From this it would emerge that the Trial Chamber concluded that Kvocka was the camp commander because he made this comment of objection and try to put the situation right and stop it. Kvocka on one occasion said, "Had I hidden in a mouse-hole, I won't be here in court today. Nobody would have seen me, whereas I did my best to help, help wherever I could. I helped wherever I could. I brought in packages publicly, although at the time that wasn't a good thing to do." But I'll go on to speak later on about the system and problems of intent and consciousness. So the ten minutes that you spend there when you don't know the structure of the camp, the hierarchy in the camp and you know nothing; and then you reach the conclusion that Kvocka was the camp commander. What are the grounds for you to do that within the space of ten minutes, a fact which here and now can describe this person as a war criminal? He is married to a Muslim. He has two sisters married to Muslims. He is part of the multi-ethnic community in the area. His daughter married a Croat while he was in the Detention Unit and he was able to see his grandchild when he released from the Detention Unit for the first time. So on the basis of these ten minute assessments and not any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness, but witness Nusret Sivac who said he saw Kvocka in July, walking around in July, and issuing orders. But we have dealt with all the witnesses by name. Witness A, we discussed her at length here yesterday. Your Honours, that witness spent in Omarska just two days, two days with Kvocka in Omarska. She was arrested between the 16th and the 18th. Kvocka was absent, according to conclusions of the Trial Chamber. He came to work on the 20th. He worked for two days. On the third day he spent walking around and left. So a witness that was completely unreliable for the central part of the indictment against Radic, with all the confusion that she entered into the courtroom, seems to be reliable enough for the conclusion to be made that when he had a problem, he would go and contact them. And then the Trial Chamber entered in brackets the individuals, although that is not something that exists in the transcript itself. But they were on duty. We are not questioning at any time that Kvocka was on duty. We're not questioning or contesting that his status for layman could have appeared to be different. We are not even contesting an assertion made by the Trial Chamber that Kvocka said himself that he supported his commander of the police station. Yes, he did; but not in persecution, not in crimes, but in performing the general police duties. At the beginning of June, they were given assignments, an assignment that they believed to be legitimate that was pursuant to police procedure and rules and applied to the circumstances. And that somebody in May, at the end of May 1992, an ordinary man, 99 per cent of the inhabitants at this time in May 1992 could not have even dreamt of the evils that were to befall their age and they couldn't believe that. People just didn't believe that there would be a war. People didn't believe there'd be a conflict of any kind. There was propaganda. There was fear. So under such circumstances those are the circumstances in which these people had to work. Your Honours, I'm not going to dwell on the facts any more, and I consider that at this point in time, if you were to compare all the statements that you have had and you have heard, you will be able to conclude that the Trial Chamber erred. With respect to matters of law, I accept the positions taken by the Appeals Chamber in the Ojdanic trial, Ojdanic case where it defined -- how much time have I got left? Where it defined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You have twenty minutes. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. That will be enough. I accept the position taken of the joint criminal enterprise which in a certain way was accepted by practice and proved by practice through this Tribunal that it is a form of responsibility and liability and that certain standards should be applied. And it is also in part acceptable what the -- what was ruled in the Tadic trial and Tadic judgement, except that we don't think that there are differences in the two groups. It is the type of case and not the elements which make up this second-instance judgement. But what we wish to contest here is this: Kvocka, or rather the Trial Chamber, absolutely did not prove Kvocka's awareness, knowledge, intent necessary for this undertaking, enterprise to be valid. But I have to say that on -- Kvocka spent 17 days in Omarska. He was there for 17 days. And during those 17 days, there was a four-day interruption on two occasions. So from the 29th to the 2nd, then he had four days off. And then he was there for another ten days, then he had another four days off. And then he was sent away from Omarska. This itself shows that he was not able to view or be conscious of everything that was going on, let alone share any intent. And I should like to caution and draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to the fact that Kvocka was expelled from Omarska camp. He was sent away from Omarska camp because of his relationship towards his cousins and relatives, because of the packages he brought in quite openly and publicly as a demonstration. The Trial Chamber says that this was limited assistance. That is absolutely true, because it was the time of economic crisis when you didn't have any flour or cooking oil or any basics, any foodstuffs, because Prijedor was under a blockade. But he brought in the things that people had been sent, the packages that people were sending in to the detainees, and many witnesses testified to that. Many testified to that. As opposed to others, he did this openly because he thought that nobody had the right to restrict people bringing in packages. That was his first fault. His second fault seems to be that he was married to a Muslim lady and that his sisters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, from your allotted time, would you be proposing to leave a little space for the Judges in case they want to ask any questions? Mr. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. And for that reason, Your Honour, I'm going to speak about intent within the frameworks of a joint criminal enterprise and intent within the frameworks of persecution. I'm going to speak to the issue in the same way. So the elements I'm now going to speak about is the -- indicates the absence of discriminatory intent and absence in support of a joint criminal enterprise for both these areas. Kvocka is married to a Muslim lady. His two sisters are married to Muslim men. He has open sympathies for Muslims. He helps Muslims, and at that time that was the greatest sin. Before the Trial Chamber, we presented proof by which witness Basrak Lazar who was a policeman, he was a policeman let me repeat, he testified and said the following: "When Kvocka arrived and began working in the Tukovi police station," it's a territorial police station where there is no active duty policemen he called the commander of the police station and -- or the commander of the police station rang them up and said, "Be wary. Be careful. You've got an enemy coming in." And also we had another witness Samardzija Zdravko, testifying before this Tribunal. He was a security -- member of the security station and Mr. Drljaca asked him to intercept Kvocka's telephone conversations because he thought he was an enemy of the ideas pursued at the time by Simo Drljaca. Then we had another witness testifying. I think his name was Kondic, who was confirmed here that Kvocka was threatened quite openly. We had the testimony of a female witness, and she was a Bosniak and she confirmed that throughout the war -- Your Honours from, this perspective it is difficult for you to understand, but she said that a young man, a Bosniak, spent the whole war in Miroslav Kvocka's house and slept in the same room with his son Sinisa. She said that here in court. She testified about that, the lady witness did. The lady spoke here of this, and unfortunately she had to leave the country after the war and is now residing in Sweden. She came here all the way to Sweden [as interpreted] to testify that Kvocka had no discriminatory intent whatsoever. On the contrary, Your Honours. Only the Trial Chamber concluded itself that Kvocka intervened benevolently whenever he could. It was the year 1992. Kvocka stood up in front of a barrel of a gun. Buses had come and one person whose brother had been killed recently started shooting, there were two or three armed Bosniaks around, and Kvocka stood up to them and stopped the shooting. There are witnesses to this: Rosic Branko, Milenko Rosic, Miroslav and another Misic. The person who was wounded in that shooting also gave an affidavit. And now can you imagine this irony and derogation of all legal principles, the Prosecution accusing Mr. Kvocka of being co-perpetrator in the murder of these persons when he stood in front of a barrel of an enraged man and saved all those people with his body? In the indictment, however, the sentence co-perpetrator -- the words co-perpetrator stay, and he was convicted of it. In facts and in conclusions, there were no -- there was no basis to convict Kvocka as participant in a joint criminal enterprise. You will see, because I don't have much time now, the analysis of the murders. The Prosecution itself admits that Kvocka cannot remain as perpetrator of sexual persecution or the perpetrator of three murders even if the indictment remains standing. We already have the judgement of the Trial Chamber saying that Kvocka can be considered responsible only for the time that he spent in the camp. Not a single murder, if I have come to murders now, happened in Omarska while Kvocka was there. The murder of Becir Medunjanin happened when Kvocka was on a four-day leave. The only murder in Omarska that happened while Kvocka was around was on the 12th of June. But even that was a night when he was on duty. How can Kvocka be considered a perpetrator or co-perpetrator? Here we believe that the principle of joint criminal enterprise should apply to each murder in particular, not murders taken together. All this is elaborated in our brief in great detail, but I have to refer to the judgement of the Trial Chamber in the Blagoje Simic case. In that case we had a Crisis Staff. The issues were similar. The Trial Chamber concluded that there was a joint criminal enterprise. Do you know what standard was set? The standard was Crisis Staff. Blagoje Simic and below. The high-ranking Simo Zaric who was deputy commander of the Security Service who, according to the findings of the Trial Chamber, conducted investigations and questionings, Miroslav Tadic who participated in exchanges of the population, people who were in a way removed from Republika Srpska, they were not convicted as members of the joint criminal enterprise. I'm only trying to say that here in this case we have a very different level. You have in front you our briefs. Even if we accepted that the Trial Chamber was correct as to the facts that Kvocka was the functional equivalent of the deputy commander of the guard service, I believe that that level compared to the organisation can serve as sufficient presumption of his role in the camp by the standards of the trials after the World War II. The lowest level of security, I repeat, was the internal security within the camp, people who were unable to change anything, to change the conditions, the structure. They were only observers. And to Kvocka's great fortune, he was thrown out of there in a humiliating way, but he was still spared for watching scenes that people should never be made to watch. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I appreciate your arguments. I would turn now to my colleagues, the distinguished Judges. Yes. Vice-president Pocar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I, too, appreciated your presentation, counsel. I would like to put to you one question to try to understand fully what your position is on an issue you have raised. You said that the Trial Chamber erred in accepting as evidence the statement given by Mr. Kvocka to the Prosecution because he testified orally in court and you saw -- you said that accepting that statement as evidence entails a violation of the principle of directness of the evidence. I would like you to help me to understand the scope of your statement of your position. Is it your position that when a statement is provided to the Prosecution and the accused subsequently gives live testimony in court, the statement has to be set aside altogether or only as far as there is a contradiction between the statement and the testimony rendered in Court? In other terms, is your position that if the accused testifies in Court, any information contained in the statement he gave to the Prosecution must be checked during the direct examination and cross-examination in order to be usable as evidence, or is that your position that the statement has to be set aside only as far as it is inconsistent with the oral examination but can be used, as the case may be, to complete the information rendered orally? I would like to understand exactly what your position is. Mr. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I considered that if the accused appears as a witness, then his statement shouldn't be admitted into evidence as an exhibit, because the possibility is then open that all parties can question the witness on all facets. However, that's -- if we -- if the Trial Chamber accepts the statement, then the scope to which it can be used is brought into question by the Trial Chamber. Now, I would -- I consider that it would be in order if the Trial Chamber could accept those parts of the statement which were not the subject of cross-examination. Let me give you an example. Kvocka's statement is one sentence, and I ask Kvocka about that sentence. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution asks Kvocka about that sentence, and we spent at least 40 minutes discussing that particular sentence. And then during this conversation, we came to what the Trial Chamber found, that conclusion. I don't think we can accept the statement and not the sentence uttered, what the witness himself said. So that question has two premises, two ways of looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May in this -- in the same order of questions I ask you whether you allow for the possibility or not that the statement be used for purposes of assessing the credibility of the live testimony? Which would be your position on this point? If a contradiction emerges between the live testimony and the statement, would you allow for the possibility that the statement is used for purposes of assessing the credibility or not? I would like to have your view on this. Mr. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that cross-examination itself allows for that possibility alone, and in practice it is always the case that the witness is presented with the statement. He is informed of the statement. We quote it. We say, "You said such-and-such," and then he explains what he meant. So I think that the credibility can be tested and cleared up during a direct examination of the witness before the Trial Chamber, and that is why I consider that even in that situation, we should not -- it should not be a part of the evidence and exhibits. I don't see the difference between the credibility of the accused as a witness and an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Simic. I have now your position perfectly clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I should also like to thank you for your presentation, and I should like to receive some precisions on the following matter: My colleagues -- your colleagues who have also spoken, for Mr. Meakic they used the term chief of security of the camp. Now, you yourself said that it was the commander of the guard service, I believe. Now, the commander of the guard service, is that the same thing as a chief of security? Do they do different things or does it boil down to the same thing? And following on from that idea, in the chain of command your client was attached to who? He was under whose control? Whose control was he under? Mr. Meakic or, as you said, the commander of the guard service? Thank you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am fully conscious of the fact that the terminology that is used sometimes leads to certain dilemmas and misconceptions. Mr. Meakic was the commander of the police station department of the police station of Omarska. That was his professional job. The police station department of Omarska was given the assignment to provide external -- extraordinary security for the camp, which means people who in a certain way were under the authority and competence of Zeljko Meakic. They were assigned the task of providing extraordinary security, and within that extraordinary security Kvocka also had his task and assignment. To make things clearer to you, because I'm from the region myself, the commander of the police station department, pursuant to the law governing the police force, does not have the status of a superior officer. He is very low down on the hierarchy. But, yes, all the police in the police station department are subordinate to him. He has his commander, komandir, and the commander of the police station is superior to both Meakic, Kvocka, and all the other policemen. Above him, above the commander of the police station, we have the assistant head or assistant chief of police. The assistant chief of police and pursuant to this order he was the coordinator for the entire structure at the Omarska camp, and at the top of the pyramid there was the chief of the public security service. Now, what happened here is this: Mr. Meakic as commander of the police station department was de facto the commander for security or, rather, the leader for security, because the real term used is "leader," rukovodilac. And he was superior to Kvocka as well as to Radic and Prcac, and all the others within the composition of the security service. The Trial Chamber found that the leader of security -- that he was the leader of security, but these two things are separate. He is the commander of the police station department, and on this assignment he was the leader of security as well. And this term was officially used in the Sikirica case where we have an order or his signature as the leader for security, rukovodilac obezbedjenja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to round that question off, your client, then, in the chain of command, was he attached to the head of the security service or to the head of the department as you said? Could you be more specific? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] To both. To the one and to the other, because he was a policeman within the frameworks of this extraordinary security service. So Zeljko Meakic was command of police station department and at the same time commander of the extraordinary or leader of the extraordinary security. And it was one and the same man embodied in the same man, who was Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Mumba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Simic, following up on your response to Judge Pocar, the vice-president, on the issue of the statement taken by the Prosecution during their investigations from your client, the appellant, and also the acceptance of the status of testimony in court by your client, I just want to be clear in my mind, was this a statement which was recorded by the Prosecutor, recorded after the appellant was warned that whatever he would say may be used in evidence? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have absolutely no objection to any facets of this statement. It is legally perfect. We just raise this point of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg de Roca. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you. I have just one very short question. You said in your submissions, Mr. Simic, that Mr. Kvocka was not responsible for a murder on the 12th of June because he was on duty, and in the transcript this is what it says. Is this the correct understanding? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I wasn't following the transcript. Thank you, Your Honour. Kvocka was in Omarska. He didn't have any free days, any days off. But this did not happen during his shift. Kvocka on that day worked in the morning until 6.00. The killing happened at 6.00, and it happened when he had some hours off, if I can use that term and put it that way. It's the only killing that coincides with those 17 days to which the Trial Chamber limits itself. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you very much. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one tiny question, Mr. Simic. What about if the accused adopts his previous statement? Has it become generally admissible in court? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I built up my position on the situation that occurred with respect to Mr. Kvocka, but once again let me say that I consider this: This is a question of primacy, whether it was a direct statement to the Trial Chamber or a statement. Regardless of the situation, when you have direct testimony, it takes primacy. So direct testimony takes primacy. So the statement should not be used even if it were to the advantage of the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I mean is what is the position if in the course of the direct testimony the accused directly adopts the previous written statement. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he accepts it through his testimony and repeats it. It's a situation, in my opinion, in which there is no need for it to be introduced, because the witness has repeated his statement, his testimony. He demonstrated what he said previously to the Prosecution. But just one digression. We still claim that this is just a question of Tribunal practice, but in the statement we still claim that Kvocka never said that. I think we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I would thank you, Mr. Simic, on behalf of the Bench, and I would extend my appreciation to the interpreters for their courtesy in accommodating us beyond the usual time limit. We will adjourn now for 30 minutes. So the sitting is suspended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now we come to the last appellant. Ready, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you very much. I shall try in a way to provide an advance apology for some insufficiently elaborated qualifications that I will utter later, with the fact that I intended to finalise my text today. However, due to changes in the schedule, I have not had time. Lawyers must always have or find an excuse. I believe that on an earlier occasion, I referred to something that was said by a German lawyer, Savigny, who said that "Law is the mathematics of concepts." Complex mathematical operations have to be treated in written text, it is difficult to do orally. This legal matter at hand is very complex, I believe, and I will make use of a written text that I will read now. I have to apologise in advance to my client, Zoran Zigic, for the words with which I will begin my presentation, namely, I believe that the Trial Chamber's judgement prejudices not only Mr. Zigic -- but what affects me personally -- it is the institution of defence that is prejudiced, Defence as the institution which is indispensable to any sort of proceedings and whose role of the proceedings is on par with the Prosecution. At the first reading of the Trial Chamber's judgement, I was really flabbergasted. At no point in that judgement did I recognise myself or anything that I or any of my colleagues from other Defence teams emphasised in favour of the accused, much less that it was any use at all. After that, I tried to put myself in the shoes of somebody who knew nothing whatsoever about the case and re-read the judgement once again carefully. From that viewpoint, I arrived at the firm conclusion that with regard to the greatest part of the charges against the accused Zigic there was no defence at all, and in its defence case, Defence contributed exclusively to a conviction, more so than the Prosecution did. Finally, I came to the assessment that the Defence of Mr. Zigic was abominably bad and that was it would have been best for Mr. Zigic to have had no Defence at all. A judgement is a public document, one that is the most important in this institution. With a judgement like this, the Trial Chamber gave the public not only a terribly minimised but also a greatly distorted picture of Zigic's defence. A Court may err both in assessing facts and in applying the law, but it does not have the right to short sell the defence before the eyes of the whole world casually or deliberately. Nor it is -- nor is it in the interest of this Tribunal to have Defence teams before it made up of extraordinarily incompetent lawyers. It is a matter of course that the Trial Chamber has great discretion in interpreting Defence arguments, but it is obliged to interpret them within a framework that is fair. However, the repercussions of such an approach hit the accused Zigic the hardest. A few words about the standards that the Trial Chamber applies or may apply.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. "Appeals Chamber applies or may apply."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already expressed our doubts as to the importance of the assertion the Trial Chamber constitutes in some way a lie detector and that it is in a better position to assess the credibility of a witness sitting before them in the witness box. In our reply to the consolidated Prosecution respondent's brief, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which we submitted on the 10th of December, 2002, we have already provided a detailed explanation of the inadmissible nature of the standard any reasonable person and even any reasonable trier of fact. We believe that the subsequent practice of the Appeals Chamber still, albeit tacitly, confirmed in every way the inadmissibility of this standard which is mentioned as far back as the judgement of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case. The standard of any reasonable trier of fact, in our conviction, is a standard designed for the purposes of a jury trial system, which is not our case. It is our belief that these standards should not go below the level prescribed by Article 13 of the Tribunal's Statute. However, we hope sincerely that even with lower standards the decision that we appealed will be changed, will be varied. In the same decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case, paragraph 64, reference is made as in some other decisions such as Kunarac Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 39, reference is made to the fact that two Judges, both acting reasonably, may arrive at differing conclusions based on the same evidence. That is perfectly true, and that is something that we have to say is normal. However, at the same time, this is contrary to the essence of law itself and the basic legal principles. It cannot be good or admissible that one or more persons charged or convicted of certain identical acts may be convicted or acquitted or sentenced differently only because of the different views of the Judges. Something like that is absolutely inadmissible both in the civil law system and in the common law system. In the latter, this is particularly striking, although precedents are related primarily to law, not facts. We therefore pointed out in one of our earlier submissions then that when such a situation arises wherein different Judges derived considerably differing conclusions from the same evidence, the process cannot stop there. Additional criteria must be sought and established to resolve that situation. However, we later came to the conclusion that such criteria have been in existence for a long time now and that they are very simple. Namely, if any Judge who is called upon to decide, acting reasonably, arrives at a different conclusion based on the same evidence, that then is indubitable proof that there is reasonable doubt and that the decision made is not beyond reasonable doubt. Admittedly, the application of this criterion is problematic in the case of majority decision-making. We can follow up on this with the standard in dubio pro reo, which means that if Judges express a certain reasonable doubt, they should incline to a solution which is more favourable to the accused. Similar is true in cases of differing legal evaluations. If several Judges acting reasonably come up with differing legal solutions, the final solution should be in keeping with the principle favor re. There has been frequent reference to these principles so far but within the framework of problems that arise at only one level, that is in proceedings before a Trial Chamber or before an Appeals Chamber. However, they should certainly apply to cases of discrepancy between two judicial instances such as the Trial Chamber and Appeals Chamber. These principles simultaneously express also the rights of the accused, which may not be denied to him at any point during the proceedings. Bearing in mind the large scope of the evidence adduced, the overall material and the lengthy transcript available to the Trial Chamber, the judgement in its part referring to the accused Zigic is very terse. We cannot but note that the indictment with its annexes is longer than the disposition of Zigic's conviction, which is a curiosity per se. This indicates that the Trial Chamber selected and quoted only that which it considered to be of the greatest importance, such -- in such a way as a point which was the most important regarding Zigic's responsibility and as an introduction into his responsibility. The Trial Chamber accepted and quoted in paragraph 548 something that constitutes an error of the Language Services. Thus the fundamental assessment on Zigic's responsibility was founded by the Trial Chamber on an erroneous translation. This has been discussed following our request for corrigenda of transcript and judgement of 24 December 2001. A joint report of the parties based on the report of the Language Services was submitted to the Appeals Chamber. We think that the Appeals Chamber should make a separate decision on this, a special finding, before proceeding with the appeals hearing. As the case goes, Zigic did not beat Rizah Hadzalic as we read in paragraph 548 of the judgement, but rather Rezak and Began, which is what the correction of the Language Services says. The difference is huge. Rizah Hadzalic is a symbol of the suffering of Muslims in Omarska which the Trial Chamber heard from witnesses at least 50 times. Guards beat him to death only because he uttered the word "bujrum," and that happened on the 12th of July, 1992, as we read in paragraph 445 of the judgement. Therefore, the Trial Chamber was wrongly under the impression that Zigic partook in this. This error helped create the wrong impression that Zigic beat up more people in Omarska and that his presence was more frequent and covered a greater period of time; whereas Zigic was in Omarska only once, and it happened to be just when Rezak and Began were being beaten. Zigic admitted himself that he beat one of them, and the judgement established that he didn't beat the other at all. Generally speaking, our request for corrigenda covers other misquotations of witnesses that can be read in the judgement of the Trial Chamber. At several points, the judgement quotes witnesses as saying things they didn't actually say. These corrections were rejected with the explanations that the points in issue were conclusions of the Trial Chamber to be evaluated by the Appeals Chamber. We find that decision erroneous. We believe, on the contrary, that it's very dangerous to write conclusions in a judgement in the form of non-existent witness testimony. It is a form of falsification. We must note, we cannot help noting, that such cases occurred here always to the detriment of the Defence. On the other hand, for the Appeals Chamber to be able to work normally at all, it is necessary to know what exactly the witness said and what the Trial Chamber concluded. Witness testimony should not be subject to change by anyone, whereas conclusions of the Trial Chamber are subject to evaluation by the Appeals Chamber, and the Appeals Chamber in this evaluation may arrive at different conclusions. Therefore, we kindly ask the Appeals Chamber to bear in mind that numerous quotations of witness testimony in the judgement are quoted wrongly. However, in addition to the judgement, the other side, that is, the Prosecution, unfortunately made another large contribution to distorting what the witnesses really said and what makes up the contents of the evidence. At this point we will only refer to our submission titled "Process against intentional misinterpretation of witness statements by the Prosecution" filed on the 11th of July, 2001. On that occasion, the Prosecution admitted to the mistakes that we pointed out, explaining that they were not made intentionally. But they only continued their old practice before we intervened again just before the end of Zigic's defence case before the Trial Chamber. However, bearing in mind the context of these errors, they can hardly have been made accidentally. Thus, for instance, if a witness explicitly said that the incident between Zigic and Hasan Karabasic occurred outside the complex in Trnopolje, why did the Prosecution serve to the Trial Chamber a version wherein the same witness said that the same incident occurred within the complex in Trnopolje? Was it an attempt to deceive the Trial Chamber? Judging by the non-reaction of the Trial Chamber, the defeat is seemingly success. Unfortunately, this kind of practice continued even before the Appeals Chamber, although we have to admit in a smaller degree. But every instance of it is very dangerous. Thus, for instance, in their consolidated reply to the appeals of the accused, the Prosecution added in Zigic's case four non-existent beatings which the Trial Chamber allegedly found or established in its judgement. We treated this in detail in our reply to the consolidated Prosecution respondent's brief filed on the 10th of September, 2002. Why, for instance, did the Prosecution write there that the Trial Chamber found in paragraph 530 of the judgement that Zigic seriously beat up Silvio Saric when the judgement did not establish this? And it is even less true that Zigic had any contact with Silvio Saric whatsoever. Why is the Prosecution doing this? We have to view this conduct in the light of the fact that the Prosecution interrupted the testimony of their most reliable witnesses in an unfair way, those witnesses being Azedin Oklopcic and Abdulah Brkic, just at the moment when they were supposed to testify about the murder of Becir Medunjanin, knowing that these witnesses in their previous statements absolutely ruled out Zigic from this event. We can add to this conduct the concealment of a witness like Witness KV1 whom we heard yesterday. It is not our intent today to critique the Prosecution. Moreover, we have only the most sincere regret about presenting this before a team of the Prosecution to whom these things cannot be ascribed personally. Our intention is to point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm interested in your statement that you're not embarking on a critique of the Prosecution's approach. Would it be helpful if you told us what's wrong with the judgement, why we should reverse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but I would appreciate it very much if you would allow me to finish this. It's only one sentence. Based on this conduct we derived certain conclusions which can affect the whole fate of this process. It is our intention to point out to the trial -- to the Appeals Chamber two very important things. First, every interpretation of evidence and the judgement by the Prosecution has to be treated with the greatest caution, and that has been a factor that has prejudiced the position of the Defence, especially before the Trial Chamber. And second, in this conduct there are elements of what we call abuse of process, which could lead to a mistrial. To prosecute somebody and then to resort to tricks in order to get a conviction can really be qualified in this way. In our further presentation, we shall stick to the sequence and the grounds for appeal with much less digression and with proper grouping of the grounds as we indicated them in our brief of the 3rd of July, 2002. We drafted it according to the order of the Pre-Appeal Judge requiring us to decisively indicate and enumerate grounds of appeal. The 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 18th, 19th, 42nd, 44th and 45th ground of appeal relate to the conviction of Zigic for all murders committed in Omarska, all tortures committed in Omarska, and his participation in the so-called joint criminal enterprise as well as the acts allegedly committed in Keraterm and Trnopolje. We link the conviction for all murders and all tortures in Omarska with the joint criminal enterprise only conditionally, because we cannot see them with certainty either in the indictment or in the judgement of the Trial Chamber. We provided a detail rationale for this in our response to the consolidated Prosecution reply filed on 10 September 2002. On this occasion, we should only like to reiterate that the Trial Chamber had a discriminatory approach towards Zigic compared to other accused because Zigic is the only one who was convicted for the entire period of existence of the Omarska complex, although even according to the indictment he spent only a couple of hours in Omarska. The Trial Chamber did not even adhere to what it established as a principle in paragraph 349 of its judgement. The other accused who, unlike Zigic, were employed in Omarska, were convicted only for the time of their engagement, not before or after it. In the judgement, the concept of joint criminal enterprise is elucidated in an extremely incoherent contradictory and inadmissible way. It is our firm impression that the Trial Chamber understood this concept as a separate act which we must point out does not exist in the Statute of the Tribunal. Furthermore, neither from the indictment or from the judgement are the accused able to find out to what act the joint criminal enterprise relates, if it is understood as a form of responsibility, whether it relates to persecutions, murders, tortures, or all of the three. Was Zigic convicted of all these acts doubly? Once when they were qualified as joint criminal enterprise, and the second time when they were qualified as "ordinary" persecutions, murders, and torture? And then how come in addition to murders and tortures in June 1992 all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the murders and tortures in July and August were laid at Zigic's door only after the end of the Prosecution case, after the appearance of all of 50 witnesses and when Zigic was no longer able to ask them any questions about it? All in all, Zigic's conviction for all murders and all tortures that occurred in Omarska, including the time when he was lying in hospital or when he was gaoled in Banja Luka may inflict much greater damage to the Tribunal than to Zigic, if that is comparable at all. He is also convicted for his participation in the sexual abuse of women, although at the time he was totally unaware that there were any women in Omarska. This conviction without guilt could be a synonym of injustice for the future generations of lawyers throughout the world. Another principled objection to the construction of the joint criminal enterprise is borne out by our position that this construction, and especially as it was presented in this case, represents a step back even in comparison to Nuremberg. And this can be said in other words, too, and that is that the Nazis, although without a doubt they had a common plan and a common purpose, were in a more favourable position than the persons accused were here. The Nuremberg judgement, in actual fact, calls this construction common plan and conspiracy. It recognised its applicability only with respect to the waging of an aggressive war, and with respect to war crimes and crimes against humanity, acquittals were pronounced because with respect to those crimes, this was not provided for expressly by the Nuremberg Charter.
