In the chapter entitled, "The law of the Charter," and the sub-heading of the law as to the common plan or conspiracy, among the other things it is stated: "[In English] The Tribunal will therefore disregard the charges in count 1 that the defendants conspired to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity and will consider only the common plan to prepare, initiate and wage aggressive war." [Interpretation] The following grounds for appeal, numbers 4, 5, 6, 22 and 23, as they are set out in our submission of the 3rd of July, 2002, relate to the killing of Becir Medunjanin and the torture of Witness T. This part of the indictment and judgement we deal with in detail in our final trial brief and in our appeal and reply to the Prosecutor's response to our appeal. We feel that we voiced at least a hundred objections, but in the judgement there is not a single response to any one of them, and that is why we should like to remind you of just a few of them here and now. It is a basic fact to be borne in mind that Zigic was never present at the "white house" in Omarska when the act took place. The judgement is based on the testimony of two witnesses, Witness T and the testimony of Fadil Avdagic as opposed to the testimony of several other otherwise very reliable witnesses who were eyewitnesses that Zigic was not there at all. And what is even worse, both those testimonies are incorrigibly deficient and are at odds with one another. Both witnesses claim to have been eyewitnesses, and as victims, they directly participated in the events is what they said. However, Witness Fadil Avdagic claims that Zigic or, rather, the person who killed Becir Medunjanin was -- had reddish blonde, dyed hair, and all the witnesses subsequently were asked about the colour of Zigic's hair, and they always said that it was dark, particularly during those days, especially dark, that he was 190 metres [as interpreted], whereas Zigic is of a medium height of 180 centimetres and was slim at the time. They said that he wore gloves without fingers. Zigic couldn't have worn gloves like that because he had a large bandage on his left land because his finger had been amputated, and we attached medical documentation and expert findings to bear that out. And then they said that he wore an earring in the shape of a cross. We also proved that Zigic never had his ears pierced. Witness T, describing the same person, goes on to claim that they had black hair, or dark hair, that they were about 180 centimetres tall. He says he didn't notice any fingerless gloves on his hands or a bandage. According to Witness T, all this happened at night. Witness Avdagic, like other eyewitnesses, claimed that it happened during the day. There are a series of other large-scale inconsistencies between the testimonies of these two witnesses, allegedly eyewitnesses, and we pointed those discrepancies out. How then can the judgement say what it does in paragraph 605 and claim that Fadil Avdagic corroborated the testimony of Witness T? On the other hand, Witness T claims that he didn't know Zigic at all and that the person -- a person called Samir Esefin in Omarska told him that that killer and torturer's -- that his name was Zigic. Therefore, Witness T, in that respect, is a hearsay witness. Was this man Samir there at all? What did he see? Did he actually know Zigic? No attempt was made to establish any of those things ever. And to this we should add a capital fact. Witness T, after two days spent in the courtroom and after insistently repeating and insisting to -- when asked by the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber could not recognise Zigic in the courtroom. And he would have to have recognised him, had Zigic really been in the "white house" at the time, because allegedly Zigic spent a lot of time beating him and mistreating him and his father on two consecutive days. Apart from that, the Defence proved that Witness T was otherwise highly unreliable and that he lied with respect to several significant details. And that is all upon which the Trial Chamber bases its judgement of Zigic and his conviction of him for the killing of Becir Medunjanin and the torture of Witness T. However, for this Defence team, that is just the beginning of the story about the trial for these two acts. Contrary to these statements, we have the statements and testimonies of all the other witnesses, mostly Prosecution witnesses who said that Zigic in no way participated in the killing of Becir Medunjanin and the torture of Witness T. We would even say that the most credible witness by far, Prosecution witness, was Azedin Oklopcic, which the judgement mentions and accepts in 27 places. That witness knew Zigic very well, and judging by his testimony, he wasn't favourably disposed towards him at all. However, as an eyewitness of the killing of Becir Medunjanin and the torture of Witness T, he expressly claims that Zigic was not present during that act and that in no way did he participate in it. The Trial Chamber does not expound why they don't believe him when he says that and why they would believe him in all the other 27 cases if, with respect to this crucial event where he was a very close eyewitness, that they do not believe him. Witness Abdulah Brkic, also a close eyewitness of this event, is the second-most credible, if I can put it that way, witness. The judgement mentions him nine times. He is believed with respect to everything. The only thing that he is not believed on is that Zigic was not present in the "white house" when the murder was committed of Becir Medunjanin and the torture of Witness T took place. Therefore, the same as with witness Azedin Oklopcic, the same thing happens here. Two consistent and very clear direct eyewitnesses. Both were Prosecution witnesses mentioned in the judgement and accepts their testimony and notes this in 36 places, expressly claim that Zigic did not commit this murder. However, when it came to convicting Zigic for the murder of Becir Medunjanin, no pieces of evidence seem to have been relevant. However, that is not all. Those two testimonies were substantiated in all respects by Defence witnesses, DD10 -- and when it comes to convicting the accused, the judgement seems to believe them -- as well as the testimony of Witnesses DD5 and Prosecution witness Mrkalj Edin. The Defence asked that some other witnesses from Omarska be heard who were otherwise Prosecution witnesses in other cases, such as for example Witness R from the Tadic trial; Mesinovic Sabahudin and Hrncic Faruk whose written statements confirm everything that witnesses Oklopcic and Brkic stated. But they didn't come across the understanding of the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber on that score. All it did do was to succeed in having Exhibit D2/12 -- although in formal terms it didn't succeed there either because it was tendered as a Kos exhibit. As I was saying, to have this included in a very detail way, that is the testimony of Witness R in the Tadic case. However, this piece of evidence is not mentioned anywhere in the judgement itself. The trial itself relating to this part of the indictment was a real scandal which at first glance did not occur only thanks to the very conciliatory and restrained conduct on the part of the Defence. Perhaps this stance did unfortunately contribute to the condemnation. It all began by the fact the representative of the Prosecution, Mr. Keegan, interrupted his own witness Azedin Oklopcic when the man started speaking about the killing of Becir Medunjanin in Omarska. Then on the 31st of August in the year 2000 the Trial Chamber, after a response by witness Abdulah Brkic to the effect that he knew about the facts surrounding the killing of Becir Medunjanin, prevented the Defence and prohibited the Defence from examining Brkic Abdulah on that subject any further, giving the explanation that the topic could not be discussed and that the witness, although he already said that he knew about the event, couldn't be asked any questions about it. And this is done again following an objection raised by Mr. Keegan. Brkic spoke about the sufferings in Omarska, and the killing of Medunjanin was one of the major events. Apart from that the trial is called the Omarska case, and the killing of Medunjanin is the only killing in Omarska for which somebody was accused of -- separately. And the only person accused for the killing in Omarska was not allowed -- did not allow the Defence counsel to question the witnesses pursuant to the Trial Chamber decision, witnesses who had already said they knew about the event. Therefore, the Defence was prohibited from doing the most elementary things, whereas it allowed the Prosecution to do what it saw fit -- even when it went so far as badgering the Defence witnesses. And so, for example, it allowed the Prosecution to question Dusanka Andjelkovic, a witness and doctor testifying to the circumstances of the death of Drago Tokmadzic in 1992, and to ask her about the political involvement in 2001 of a person who had absolutely nothing to do with anything -- any cases before the Tribunal. Realising what it had done, the Trial Chamber, the very next day, on the 1st of September, 2000, nonetheless decided, this Defence team, to continue its examination of witness Abdulah Brkic with respect to the killing of Becir Medunjanin. However, as it states -- it is stated in the transcript, Brkic, in the meantime, had contacts with Mr. Keegan, which had as its consequence that he somewhat changed his previous written statement in which it says that another individual slit Medunjanin's throat before the eyes of this witness and that Medunjanin died on the spot as a result; and that the witness even stood in a pool of Medunjanin's blood. And Zigic was not in Omarska at all at that time. However, even after these altered details, Brkic's firm statement stood, that Zigic was not in the "white house" when the killing of Medunjanin took place and the torture of Witness T took place. This scandalous conduct is invigorated by the interpretation of Brkic's statements in the judgement in footnote 975 attached to paragraph 604. It is said that Brkic did not know whether Medunjanin died on that particular day or not, and that is an alteration to what he said after the testimony was interrupted and after he had talked to Mr. Keegan. It is also stated that Zigic was in Omarska on that particular day. That is changed testimony as well, under the previously stated circumstances, newly arisen circumstances. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I take it that the record shows that the witness did speak to Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. I think you have that in the transcript and that it is not a contestable point. I can give you the number of the transcript, the LiveNote line, et cetera. Perhaps just an additional piece of information. I would not say that was contrary to the Rules because the testimony of this witness had been concluded on that day. We were not allowed to ask him on this crucial matter, but he was no longer bound by the solemn declaration. He had completed his testimony. So that is not the aspect of this matter that we wish to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate the explanation, Mr. Stojanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Similarly, it was stated that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Zigic was in Omarska that day. That is an altered statement under the circumstances I expounded a moment ago. However, the Trial Chamber intentionally left out the fact that Brkic expressly stated that Zigic, during that event, which took place entirely in the "white house," was not in the "white house" himself. And furthermore, that he had not seen Zigic that whole day in Omarska at all, as well as that he just saw Zigic in Omarska on one occasion, and that was on the second day during the torture of Witness AK and others. Finally, the day of 7 June 2000, and the identification of Zigic in the courtroom by Witness T, maybe as a climax. This identification was part of the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution. In response to the question, asked twice, Which row is Zigic sitting in, Witness T twice responded, "I'm not sure." We remind you that in view of the circumstances of the occurrence of the events and of the trial, it was expected of this witness to recognise him. The witness was a high-ranking military officer, an activist, and he had ample opportunity to see and watch Zigic umpteen times. However, it must be that his conscience woke up in the courtroom because the face of the person who did torture him and killed his loved one was simply not in the courtroom. And then something unbelievable happened. The President of the Trial Chamber takes over from the Prosecution the job of identification and continues to question the witness on points that the witness responded to more than once. Before this Tribunal, it has been prohibited a thousand times to ask questions that witnesses have already replied to, and it is the duty of precisely the President of the Chamber to enforce this. Zigic's Defence counsel is on his feet, intending to object. The Presiding Judge does not allow this objection and continues, for the umpteenth time, to ask Witness T where Zigic is sitting in the courtroom. How can we explain that the Defence is not allowed to object, especially in situations as scandalous as this one. And then that same Trial Chamber in these proceedings grants the conviction of Zigic for murder, torture, persecution in Omarska and even participation in a joint criminal enterprise in Omarska. It grants them on conduct of this sort. But this conduct is certainly not isolated. It fits within the context of everything that had been said previously regarding the conviction for the murder of Becir Medunjanin and the torture of Witness T, but also within the context of all the other irregularities. Despite all that, however, Witness T did not finally identify Zigic, and by all and every rule, his identification should have been over the moment when he first said, "I'm not sure." Grounds for appeal number 7, number 8, and number 9 relate to the conviction for the murder of Emsud Bahonjic. This has been sufficiently in our enactments, especially in our appeal. The judgement deals with this incident on less than one page. It deals with it in combination with the murder of Sead Jusufagic as a single event in keeping with the obviously inaccurate statement of Witness N, whereas the remaining 20 testimonies indicate clearly that Sead Jusufovic had been murdered, had been killed before Emsud Bahonjic arrived at Keraterm. In fact, this Defence does not accept that on the charge of murder of Emsud Bahonjic there was a real trial at all. A conviction was pronounced, but there was no trial. A trial is a process which necessitates the participation of the Defence. The Defence must be present also in the most important part of the trial, in the judgement, as proof that in whatever way, the Court appreciated its arguments and evidence presented. In our judgement, the Defence is absent. All the six Defence witnesses who had been called to testify on the death of Bahonjic, all the Defence arguments, all the statements of Prosecution witnesses which favour the Defence were ignored completely. Not a single reference is made to them. Nor is there a reference to the medical findings on the injuries of Emsud Bahonjic as Exhibit D4/24, or the two Prosecution exhibits such as 3/270, and 3/271, which also relate to medical documents on the injuries of Emsud Bahonjic. All in all, the transcript relating to Defence witnesses comprises about 1.000 pages, and one must add to that over a hundred pages of our arguments and exhibits, all of which went unnoticed in the few lines dedicated to the Defence in the rationale given in the judgement. Therefore, we invoke here all those things that the Trial Chamber considered to be non-existent. So we are now basically in a situation where we have the first real trial for the murder of Emsud Bahonjic. But by the same token, we have been deprived of the right to a two-tier trial and of the opportunity to say anything at all about any reason for non-admission of Defence arguments and evidence. However, even those things that the Trial Chamber does invoke are certainly not sufficient to convict Zigic for the murder of Emsud Bahonjic. In the worst scenario for Zigic, he could be convicted for participating in the beating of Bahonjic. We will set aside for the moment the fact that two Prosecution witnesses did not identify Zigic in the courtroom, although they had allegedly known him for years. We shall leave and set aside the fact that some of the witnesses from Keraterm remarked him for the scar which, as was proven later, he acquired after Keraterm was closed. We shall set aside the fact that they were at Bahonjic's side all the time without noticing that he was taken to the hospital twice, bandaged there, and many other deliberate or accidental untruths. All those witnesses referenced by the judgement said that many people jointly or separately beat Emsud Bahonjic on many various occasions in an interval of ten days and that Emsud died several days after his last beating. One cannot see from their testimonies when Zigic participated in that and to what degree. Moreover, as evidenced from the testimony of Ervin Ramic, Zigic participated in this in the beginning, before the medical check-up of the 15th of June, 1992. This check-up resulted in a medical finding, Exhibit D4/24, saying that at that moment, the injuries were far were lethal. From the testimony and statements of these same witnesses, we see that one other person alone, without Zigic, beat up Bahonjic at least ten times. It is also in evidence that Predrag Banovic, without Zigic's participation, beat up Bahonjic so badly on one occasion that Bahonjic's whole left side of the head was completely deformed. In this context, we requested the application of a number of standards established in the judgement of the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case, paragraph 458 of that judgement in particular, one of them being whether in that context only reasonable possibility is that Bahonjic, after several days and numerous beatings, succumbed precisely from the injuries incurred from Zigic's beating, or there are other reasonable possibilities. But as we already said, the Trial Chamber completely ignored all the arguments of the Defence, including this one. In its intention to ignore the arguments of the Defence, the Trial Chamber wasn't even bothered by the fact that it had to ignore the decisions of the Appeals Chamber as well. Finally, on top of an unclear actus reus and especially the causal link between the conduct of Zoran Zigic and the occurrence of death of Emsud Bahonjic, the issue of mens rea of the accused Zigic was ignored completely as well; in other words, whether Zigic knew on the condition that he had beaten Bahonjic at all that this beating, his beating alone, would result ten days later in the death of Emsud Bahonjic. Your Honours, I am now moving on to other grounds. Would this perhaps be a convenient time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. We shall suspend --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's on. I said thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. I propose that we now take a suspension until this afternoon at the appointed time, which will be near to 2.30. Thank you very much. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This sitting is resumed. Mr. Prosecutor, my information is that you would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I would be quite brief, Your Honour. Your Honour, in the light of the various allegations that are being made against the conduct of the Prosecution at the trial, the Prosecution is concerned that some of the allegations are not given the level of specificity that is required in the context of citation and in the context of exactly what has been referred to. As much as in fact an oral hearing is in fact a creature of response in that it basically it would entail simply responding to arguments that are in fact put forward, if these arguments are broad and general, it is very difficult for the Prosecution to respond in an adequate manner that would assist the Chamber. Apart from that specifically, I just wish to address additionally that my friend has made reference to the Prosecution consolidated reply, I think it's our response, where he says we have added four non-existent beatings which the Trial Chamber did not find. Again, we would like some -- for him to be a little more specific in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Carmona, may I suggest to you, if I were at your place, and I'm not, I would reserve that for incorporation in my address. And I would mention that I was handicapped and I -- because of lack of detailed references, if it were so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Well, indeed, Your Honours. Well, I have taken the licence to inform my friend, and he has in fact indicated that in fact he is prepared to assist in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, shall we leave it to him? Yes. Yes. Ready, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I thank you very much. If you allow me only a few words. Of course my presentation today suffers from omission of detail of all manner of kind, because it's only a summary. If we wish to be precise and provide everything that my learned friend requires, we would have to repeat the final trial brief, the appellant's brief and our reply to their consolidated response, and that would take me about three days to present in every detail what my learned friend is interested in. But even then, I would place an undue burden on the Appeals Chamber, practically, by repetition of everything that is said in these documents. Having said that, I am ready and willing to sit down with my colleague Mr. Carmona and come back to the issues I raised in my presentation. I understand that I am given leave to continue. Grounds for appeal number 10, number 11, and number 12 relating to the murder of Sead Jusufagic, Car. This conviction, too, is explained only on one page of the judgement. The judgement describes this event as a single occurrence with the murder of Emsud Bahonjic but it was told that way by only one extremely unreliable witness, as we explained in great detail; while the remaining 15 witnesses testified that it is a separate event which occurred before the arrival of Emsud Bahonjic at Keraterm. One is immediately struck by the question how is it possible that in the case of the murder of Emsud Bahonjic Defence should be completely ignored, whereas in the case of murder of Sead Jusufagic the Defence witnesses, and even the statement of -- the testimony of accused Zigic himself, be given a great number of references, more references, in fact, than the evidence adduced by the Prosecution. The answer is very simple. In the case of Emsud Bahonjic, not a single defence proof was in favour of conviction. And that is why Defence was completely ignored. While in the case of the murder of Sead Jusufagic, Defence witnesses in minor parts of their testimony spoke of things that could charge Zigic, that could incriminate Zigic. The Trial Chamber then, very carefully and without a single error, selected these minor and less important statements in favour of conviction and completely ignored the remaining 90 per cent or more of the testimony. This is not only about quantity, considering that vital and important evidence and testimony was ignored to the effect that Zigic did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not kill Sead Jusufagic. What a mechanism at work. In theory, even such a curiosity is possible, but in that case at least a convincing explanation is required. In the absence of any explanation whatsoever, such a mechanism constitutes only very firm proof of the bias of the Trial Chamber. And this trial, selective as it was, was based on very unreliable evidence. Witness N, who incriminates Zigic the most, failed to recognise him in the courtroom, although the circumstances of his testimony should have required him to do so. Witness Abdulah Brkic confirms that Zigic mistreated Sead Jusufagic, forcing him to run carrying a machine-gun but did not beat him. The judgement is largely based on the evidence of Witness Ervin Ramic, which abounds with proven untruths and who completely ignores the event wherein Zigic forced Jusufagic to run around carrying a machine-gun, an event that all the prisoners of Keraterm knew about and retold many times. He described the death of Jusufagic in a considerably different way than all the remaining 15 witnesses of both the Defence and the Prosecution. We provided a detailed explanation of this in our appeal. And why this testimony was accepted as it was the Trial Chamber failed to explain. Thus in terms of Defence evidence, there was no trial in this case either. The problem here is similar to the one with the murder of Emsud Bahonjic. Defence witnesses claim, as does Zigic himself when he provided a statement under Rule 84, that Zigic forced Car to run around with a machine-gun and that he hit him only once, kicking him from behind. In the words of these witnesses, Sead Jusufagic, also known as Car, was killed a couple of days later by completely different people, but as we have explained already, the Trial Chamber ignored everything that favoured the Defence, and this is in no way reflected in the judgement. On the other hand, all the witnesses on whose testimonies the judgement is based, although contradictory and unreliable, assert that Sead Jusufagic was beaten by many people and on many occasions. From the totality of this testimony, it is impossible to determine the contribution of Zigic to the death of Sead Jusufagic or, as his last name was then, Jusufagic. One can only perhaps draw a conclusion that Zigic participated in the mistreatment of Jusufagic or Jusufovic. However, even such testimony of witnesses in favour of the Prosecution are interpreted in the judgement in such a ludicrous and distorted way that they are sometimes unrecognisable, which fact we have mentioned in our appeal several times. So here again, viewing only the evidence on which the judgement relies, we see no proof that Zigic's actions caused the death of Sead Jusufagic, or any proof that Zigic, by any standard, had the adequate mens rea to cause the death of this person. On the other hand, the evidence adduced by the Defence, which the Trial Chamber ignored without any explanation, clearly indicate that Zigic did not kill Sead Jusufagic. We hope that at least the Appeals Chamber will consider this evidence so that its presentation not be completely futile. But the Defence must also have the right to respond to the conclusion of the Trial Chamber on this matter. The conclusions of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 623 of the judgement, to the effect that it doesn't matter who inflicted the final blow, run counter to the conclusion of the Trial Chamber in the Celebici case, paragraph 865, which was confirmed by the decision of the Appeals Chamber, namely that the accused, in an identical situation, must be acquitted if there is no absolute certainty as to who inflicted the fatal injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, can you help me to follow you on this point? I understand you to be proposing that the Trial Chamber simply did not consider the Defence witnesses to whom you're referring. Is there a difference between that proposition and the proposition that the Trial Chamber considered the evidence but rejected it? If you look at paragraph 621, what it says there in line 3: "Many witnesses called by the Defence corroborated Zigic's unsworn statement, saying that they saw Zigic beating Sead Jusufagic only once. Some testified that Zigic did not remain in the -- in Keraterm camp after the initial beating of Sead Jusufagic. According to a Defence witness, after the machine-gun incident, a group of soldiers arrived at the camp around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., after the funeral of a military officer and they called out Sead Jusufagic and beat him. The next morning, he was dead." So it looks to me as if an argument could be mounted to the effect that the Trial Chamber did avert to the Defence evidence on the point but rejected it. Is that the same as your proposition, that the Trial Chamber did not avert to the evidence at all, did not give it any consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the reference to one witness. You are quite correct in noting that. However, six Defence witnesses confirmed the testimony of that one witness, but these six are not mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. But the Trial Chamber did speak of many witnesses. In the third line of that paragraph, there is a reference to many Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour; but only one single case where they say that he forced Car to run around with a machine-gun. But it is omitted that he did not kill him. That was our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Invoking the stance of the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case, we shall raise the question: Is it reasonably possible that the death of Sead Jusufagic did not result from Zigic's actions? Even if we take into account the witnesses for the Prosecution and even more if we take into account the witnesses for the Defence, it is evident that such a possibility exists and, therefore, Zigic cannot be convicted for the murder of this person. I shall now move on to the grounds for appeal number 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17, relating to the conviction for the murder of Drago Tokmadzic. The reasons for convicting Zigic for the alleged murder of Drago Tokmadzic are given in the judgement on just half a page, paragraph 631 to paragraph 633, considerably smaller space in the judgement than was devoted to child pornography. This event was testified to by all of 13 witnesses. However, 11 witnesses whose testimony seemed to be favourable to Zigic were completely ignored, and I have to interject here with a comment that this text was written before yesterday's testimony of KV1, and we can add him to this number; out of them, all nine witnesses for the Defence and two witnesses for the Prosecution. The judgement is based only on the testimony of two witnesses, Witness Y and Witness Edin Ganic, two extremely unreliable and incredible witnesses, and what is worse, witnesses whose testimonies are completely incompatible. Even with regard to this part of the judgement, there is just the conviction. But there was no real trial, because the main element is missing, namely complete absence of 90 per cent of all evidence adduced. What is also missing is any serious analysis of the remaining 10 per cent of evidence. Despite all that, we shall take some time to remember these two witnesses on which the conviction relies in order to prove that even based on their testimony Zigic cannot be charged with this murder. Even if we take into account only what is written in the judgement, Zigic cannot possibly be co-perpetrator of the murder. Witness Y claims he was captured not later than the 24th of June, 1992, and that the same evening Drago Tokmadzic was taken out of his room into Keraterm and murdered. He was killed by soldiers in disguise who wore black masks and gloves and who, after 2300 hours that night, arrived at Keraterm in a large vehicle. That witness heard from other persons in the room that from the shining of headlights of that vehicle on the ceiling of the room, they concluded that it was Zigic coming to kill. Generally speaking, this witness was quite decisive in stating that he had never seen Zigic. Thus the judgement bases Zigic's identification in this incident on hearsay to the effect that Zigic was recognised by the way his headlights shone, as if those headlights and the light they reflect were an identifying part of the body. On the other hand, witness Edin Ganic, as follows from his statement, the statement of his father Husein Ganic and Exhibit 3/139, which constitutes a document on his admission into a hospital, arrived at Keraterm not earlier than the 29 June 1992. And he, too, claims that he was an eyewitness to the killing of Drago Tokmadzic, but he describes that murder in a completely different way than Witness Y. He says, namely, that on the 29th or the 30th of June, 1992 in the afternoon and evening hours, Banovic, Zigic, and Lajic, wearing no masks or gloves -- that is Banovic, Zigic, and Lajic, not some masked soldiers -- carried out a whole series of beatings. They had not arrived in any vehicle. They had simply been there for quite awhile. And even a Prosecution witness, AE, said that Tokmadzic had been killed by soldiers, not guards. This is the reason why the Defence carried out a detailed investigation about the moment of death of Mr. Tokmadzic and was informed by at least 20 people that Edin Ganic had arrived at Keraterm a considerable time after the death of Drago Tokmadzic and could not have possibly witnessed his killing. Some of these persons agreed to testify, and particularly important is the testimony of Dusanka Andjelkovic, the doctor who summoned by the chief of police to note the death of Drago Tokmadzic, who was, by the way, a policeman of the Serb police. The doctor did so and noted that Drago Tokmadzic had died as a result of beating that took place in the early morning of the 21st of June, 1992. That is at least eight days before the so-called eyewitness Edin Ganic arrived at Keraterm. And that Edin Ganic, on top of everything, did not know Drago Tokmadzic at all, and allegedly it was precisely Zigic who informed him that the person who had already been beaten up and whom he was able to see was called Drago Tokmadzic. Zigic disputes that he had any contact with Edin Ganic whatsoever. So this, too, is hearsay, and his testimony is hearsay. A hearsay witness is also the person who allegedly informed him. That person disputes his allegation that he informed him in the first place. Moreover, Edin Ganic does not say that Zigic beat Drago Tokmadzic at all. He only says that he instructed another person, Goran Lajic, to "finish that off," and that is written in the judgement. Whether Lajic heard this alleged instruction at all, we cannot know. And whether Lajic, as a guard, was perhaps even superior to Zigic is also questionable, as is the meaning of giving an instruction. The only thing it cannot mean is what it stands -- what it says in the judgement, namely, that the very instruction, regardless of the circumstances, a person becomes co-perpetrator. Couldn't he be an instigator or an aider and abettor or, rather, in these circumstances, somebody who cannot be held responsible at all? And what does "finish that off" mean, and why does this instruction mean kill him rather than finish the beating? From the statement of a witness victim AG given in this case, "They finish me off," it obviously means, "they beat me up." We also reminded the Trial Chamber of the stance of the Appeals Chamber from the Celebici case that conviction cannot be based on equivocal verbal statements, but as we have already mentioned, the Trial Chamber did not try this part at all. And finally, there is no evidence whatsoever that Drago Tokmadzic belonged to the opposite side in the conflict, and as a civilian at that, so that the provisions of the Statute of the Tribunal would be applicable. On the contrary. There was evidence that he was a policeman in the Serb police force and it was wearing that uniform that he was brought to Keraterm. There is also evidence that he had signed a declaration of loyalty to the Serb authorities and that he had previously himself been bringing prisoners to Keraterm, and that in terms of ethnicity he was half Serb, half Croat. The only evidence as to why he was killed is that he was a cruel Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. policeman who beat up people in the street. Even if the Serb side had thought that he belonged to the other side, which is not the case, one could not speak of the crimes that fall within the competence of the Tribunal. Namely, there is no mens rea that can replace or fill the absence of an objective and vital element such as actus reus, that the crime committed against the opposite side in the conflict. Nor is it sufficient to suspect that a person belonged to the other side. What is necessary is certain and unequivocal proof of that, which in this case is missing. This opinion is elaborated and supported by Judge Cassese in his work published in 2003 titled "International Criminal Law," Oxford University Press, page 48, and he illustrates this opinion using cases Piltz and Motosuke. The freshest and a very firm impression we have is that left by Witness KV1, obviously a Muslim who had been detained in Keraterm. With his testimony provided in rebuttal, this witness was emphatic when saying that he had neither seen nor heard Zigic during the killing of Drago Tokmadzic. He would have had to see or hear him under the circumstances if Zigic had indeed participated in this killing. Similarly, in his testimony this witness confirmed the case of the Defence that in this specific case, it was a member of Serb forces who was killed. On this issue, the balance of probabilities is certainly on the side of the Defence. However, since this is an important element of the act, we believe that even this test is not appropriate and that the Prosecution must prove that Tokmadzic belonged to the opposite side in the conflict beyond any reason doubt. The next grounds of appeal, numbers 20 and 21, relate to the torture of Abdulah Brkic. According to paragraph 685 of the judgement, Zigic was convicted also for the torture of Abdulah Brkic. The conviction stands only on the basis of the testimony of one single witness, Abdulah Brkic himself. There is no other corroborating evidence. However, Brkic himself said, and I'm quoting, "But Zigic never did me any harm. He never touched me." As we can read on page 4482 of the transcript. As a matter of fact, Zigic not only did not participate in the torture of Brkic, but he saved him from it; and that is why he is even more -- he is even harder hit by this conviction. The indictment against Zigic does not follow up on or invoke Annex D regarding count 12 which relates to the torture of Abdulah Brkic. It invokes Annex D only with reference to acts under counts 1 to 3 which we can see from paragraphs 25 and 32 of the latest indictment. Grounds for appeal number 24 relates to the torture of Witness AK. It is the position of this Defence that Zigic committed the act of cruel treatment of Witness AK, and that is confirmed by statements and testimonies of a number of witnesses as well as by the admission and repentance of Zigic himself. However, there is no evidence that he did what he did in order to discriminate against AK as a Muslim as an element of torture which is what paragraph 597 of the judgement says. On the contrary. He committed this act for purely personal reasons, as he said himself. Why would he otherwise pass up on hundreds of other Muslims in Omarska without harming any one of them before he reached AK? Follow grounds for appeal number 25, 26, and 27, relating to the torture of Witness AJ and Asef Kapetanovic, and cruel treatment of Emir Beganovic. Evidence that Zigic participated in the torture of these persons are very unreliable. Zigic did not intend to hurt Emir Beganovic. The Defence explained this in great detail in its appellant's brief, paragraphs 281 to 309. The next ground for appeal is number 28, torture of Fajzo Mujkanovic in Keraterm. The conviction of Zigic for this criminal act is based on one single piece of evidence, evidence provided by the Prosecution witness Abdulah Brkic. Four other witnesses, two proposed by the Prosecution and two proposed by the Defence are completely ignored by the Trial Chamber for the reason that they are only favourable to the Defence. At least that is our opinion. Although the witnesses of this event, these witnesses make no mention of the fact that Zigic was present during the incident. We are talking about eyewitnesses. These eyewitnesses do not mention Zigic as being present. However, even witness Abdulah Brkic states that Mujkanovic was tortured by another person, whereas Zigic was allegedly only present and did not participate in the mistreatment of Fajzo Mujkanovic as we can see from the transcript, page 4483. From this testimony, the Trial Chamber drew the conclusion that Zigic was co-perpetrator in this torture. Not an instigator, not an aider or abettor, but precisely co-perpetrator, only on the basis of the testimony that Zigic was present, present but not participating in the act, contrary to the testimony of the other four witnesses. The same Chamber, in paragraph 257 of the same judgement, determined the standards under which a person could be convicted for mere presence but only as an abettor. However, where Zigic is concerned, the Trial Chamber failed to adhere to its own standards. In addition to these standards, we would add a conviction also requires an appropriate mens rea with the person present, but the judgement, of course, did not even try to take that into consideration. The following grounds of appeal are numbers 29 and 30, and they relate to the torture of Redzep Grabic and Witness AE. In its submission of the 3rd of July, 2002, the Defence erroneously interpreted its appellant's brief of argument in stating that there were no charges against Zigic for the torture of Redzep Grabic. However, this statement, in fact, refers to Witness AE as has correctly been stated in paragraph 329 of our appellant's brief of argument. Neither in the indictment nor in any confidential supplement has Zigic been specifically charged with the torture of Witness AE, either under the pseudonym or under his real name. However, Zigic was convicted of the torture of Witness AE as stated in paragraph 691(C) of the judgement. The conviction of Zigic for the alleged beating of Redzep Grabic and Witness AE is based exclusively on the testimony of a single witness, namely, Witness AE, a witness who, although he says that he has known Zigic for a long time and that Zigic beat him, was unable to recognise Zigic in the courtroom. We are really not aware of a case anywhere in the world where someone was convicted of a serious crime on the basis of the testimony of a single witness who could not recognise the perpetrator, who could not identify the perpetrator. The Trial Chamber, aware of this, in order to strengthen this statement claims that this single witness correctly described Zigic in the given situation. First of all, as this is the only witness of the alleged event, the Trial Chamber could have reached such a conclusion only if it had been present at the event itself. And secondly, Witness AE described Zigic completely wrongly compared to some 60 or so witnesses who mention Zigic from that time. This alleged beating occurred between the 22nd and the 27th of June, 1992, and Zigic, as has been proved by the documentation adduced and other evidence, was hospitalised from the 21st to the 26th of June, 1992, and underwent major surgery. The next grounds of appeal, 31 and 32, relate to the torture of Jasmin Ramadanovic, also known as Sengin. Several witnesses mentioned that this person was beaten on several occasions in various circumstances and by various people. On one occasion, he had to be hospitalised because of serious injuries. The Trial Chamber concluded that it was Zigic who inflicted these serious injuries. However, not a single piece of evidence shows that Zigic beat Ramadanovic on that particular occasion, and there is no evidence about the gravity of the injuries he inflicted if something like this happened. The only witness supporting the conviction here was Witness N, as opposed to three witnesses who claimed that it wasn't Zigic but somebody else who did this. However, the Trial Chamber is speculating without evidence and to the detriment of the Defence by stating that these witnesses saw others -- other beatings of Ramadanovic, not the beating that Zigic participated in, that is, that they saw other events. Witness N was also very incredible, and we have given detailed reasons to support this beginning with the witness's claim that he used to recognise Zigic in Keraterm because he had a scar on his chin. During the proceedings, it was proved that Zigic acquired this scar on the 19th of August, 1992, that is, after Keraterm was disbanded. The Trial Chamber, from testimony to the effect that Zigic beat Ramadanovic because he allegedly belonged to the Green Berets draws the conclusion that he did this on the basis of ethnic, religious, and political discrimination. However, the Green Berets were an illegal paramilitary group. The following grounds of appeal are numbers 33 and 34, and they relate to cruel treatment of Hasan Karabasic. In this particular case, there is no evidence to show that this family meeting which occurred outside the Trnopolje complex or compound in which Zigic allegedly pushed his best man Hasan Karabasic with one hand because of some family arguments had any serious consequences. Karabasic was Zigic's best man, and previously he had been detained in Keraterm where Zigic looked after him in the best possible way. There is no evidence that any behaviour by Zigic caused serious suffering for the victim which would be a condition for the act of which he has been convicted. This is a truly trivial event, as the Prosecution itself states in its consolidated response to the appeals of the accused. We are not aware that in the tangible, substantial history of this Tribunal anyone has been convicted of a more trivial offence. This part of the trial, in fact, is much more significant as evidence of the unfair treatment of Zigic both by the Prosecution and by the Trial Chamber. For example, although in all the written statements supporting the indictment, Prosecution witnesses claim that this event took place on the 6th of August, 1992, Zigic has been indicted for the period from the 26th of May to the end of August, 1992, in order to create an erroneous impression that he was constantly present at Trnopolje. On the other hand, there is another example proving that in the Zigic case the Prosecution is not fighting for truth and justice. It is fighting against Zigic. For example, the testimony of a key witness, a key Prosecution witness, that this event took place outside the Trnopolje compound has been deliberately misrepresented to the Trial Chamber to make it look as if the event took place within the compound. Later on, the Prosecution, in its response to the appeals for the first time and without any explanation, claims that the witness is unclear as to this. Everything relating to this event has been dealt with in detail by the Defence in its final trial brief. However, all serious arguments are avoided in the judgement and a warped and incorrect picture of the Defence is presented. This goes so far as to use certain statements from the final trial brief of the Defence against the accused. Grounds for appeal number 35 and 36 relating to the beating of Witness V.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it would help some of us on the Bench if you would be kind enough to just refer to the particular paragraph in the impugned judgement which is under reference. As you go along and you come to particular incidents, would you kindly refer to particular paragraphs of the impugned judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I may have omitted to do so at many points during my presentation today because I was trying not to be repetitive, but I believe there are many references to the judgement, and there will be more still. In paragraphs 650 and 651 of the judgement, it is determined that Zigic beat up Witness V, and he was convicted of this as reads paragraph 691 of the judgement. However, in the indictment or the annexes to the indictment, there is no charge of beating of Witness V. Instead, in Annex D, in the section headed Persecutions, it says: "Detention in inhumane conditions in the period from the 14th of June to the 5th of August, 1992." And this is what Zigic is charged with. Zigic cannot be responsible for this act, much less for that entire period. He did not detain anyone. As far as this act is concerned, the emphasis is certainly on detention as an act of execution instead of the language of the indictment for which Zigic cannot be held responsible, the Trial Chamber convicted him for an entirely different act. In any case, when convicting for this act, the Trial Chamber omitted to determine and explain vital elements of the act, especially its discriminatory nature and intent. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Grounds for appeal number 37 and 38 and the beating of Edin Ganic. Paragraphs up to 666 of the judgement. This is based only on the testimony of Edin Ganic and his father Husein Ganic whose testimonies are mutually contradictory. Both witnesses are extremely unreliable and moreover, there is evidence in the case that they perjured themselves. Thus, for instance, Edin Ganic said he witnessed the killing of Drago Tokmadzic at Keraterm, although he arrived at Keraterm several days after that killing. Husein Ganic is a witness who did not even acknowledge the signature that had been proven to belong to him, thus disabling the Defence from questioning him about the circumstances which he described in his earlier written statement. This witness at certain moments makes statements which can in no way be attributed to a clear -- a clearly thinking, sane person. The Defence has already corroborated this opinion with an abundance of argument. When convicting Zigic for the persecution of Edin Ganic, the Trial Chamber omitted to determine the existence of discriminatory intent in Zigic. From the words of Edin Ganic himself, we can see that Zigic did not have any discriminatory intent as prescribed by Article 5 of the Statute. The next ground for appeal is number 39. Consistent pattern of conduct as evidence has not been correctly applied by the Trial Chamber, in our view. The judgement does not link any specific act to this proof. In failing to do so, the Trial Chamber violates the provision of paragraph 2 of Rule 93, which makes it obligatory to observe Rule 66. In addition, many facts were determined inaccurately and everything is based on the statement of one or two already very highly incredible witnesses. A detailed explanation of all this was provided by the Defence in paragraphs 369 to 389 of the appeals brief. It is also important to review how and why the Trial Chamber had no objection at all to the testimony of Husein Ganic. I am trying to skip certain things in order to be brief. The following grounds of appeal are 40 and 41, relating to persecutions. This act, as well as its gravity, depend in the largest part on the acts that have been discussed earlier, with additional elements such as discriminatory intent as well as systematic nature and widespread character. The judgement gives no explanation of the alleged persecution by Zigic of persons named in paragraph 691(A). Zigic was convicted for the persecution of all persons in Omarska for the entire duration of the existence of that complex, of that camp, whereas he spent only half a hour in Omarska, and there he participated in the beating of one prisoner for purely personal motivations. In addition, he had no duties whatsoever in Omarska. No responsibilities. Especially conspicuous is the absence of reasoning regarding discriminatory intent, and this has already been mentioned in dealing with other grounds for appeal. By this omission, the Trial Chamber violated its own stance stressed in paragraph 203 of the judgement, according to which it always determined the existence of discriminatory intent whenever the issue arose, although even this stance is profoundly wrong because the Trial Chamber has to determine the existence of that intent even when the issue does not arise. In Zigic's case, that stance has been violated as well. Generally speaking, the Trial Chamber pointed out several times that it does not dispose of admissible criteria regarding evaluation of discrimination in the light of Article 5 of the Statute. Let us recall only the example from paragraph 560 of the judgement. In this judgement - and that seems to be the practice in other cases as well - it is unjustifiably believed that it is sufficient to say that Serbs persecuted non-Serbs on a racial, political, or religious basis. We believe that this basis, first of all, has to be determined precisely, because persecution can be carried out for different reasons on different grounds as well. The very division into Serbs and non-Serbs is also completely groundless, especially bearing in mind that there were many non-Serbs on the Serbian side, just as there were many Serbs on the side of non-Serbs. Why would it suddenly occur to the Serbs, after several centuries of peaceful co-existence, to suddenly start persecuting Muslims? It is our deep conviction that the basic criterion for division should be into those who voted for staying within the country of Yugoslavia as opposed to those who voted to separate from Yugoslavia. There lies the basis for later discrimination. We do not dispute that later, within the context of that political division, religion and ethnicity were abused to a certain extent. It is clear to everyone that there would be no conflict as such had it not been for that division. If the Croats had voted in favour of Yugoslavia, there would never be a war in Croatia. Had the Muslims voted for Yugoslavia, there would have never been a war or persecution in Bosnia and Herzegovina, just as there had been none until that issue came up. This is something that every Muslim and every Croat would confirm. That means, furthermore, that the conflict would never break out just because some people were Serbs, other Muslims, and yet other Croats. However, in a case like this, it may be the case that there was persecution on a political basis. Had the Chamber established this, in our view this would in some way constitute a milder form of persecution as opposed to racial or religious persecution. We have already said that political persecution may even be something quite permissible, especially in a war. It is quite normal for every political party that assumes power to replace the previous political officials in power without providing any reasons or grounds for this, purely for political reasons. It is even more normal in a wartime conflict for members of the opposite side and their sympathisers not to be appointed to key positions. I have to tell you that persecution of enemies in wartime is frequently a usual imminent occurrence and may, at times, be permissible. So it is necessary to draw a distinction with what is permissible and what is not. I feel that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has not yet been fully elaborated in this respect. All this is even more complicated in a civil war such as the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina where, very often, especially in Prijedor, there was no demarcation line at the front between the warring sides, but the warring sides, as fellow citizens, were often mixed with each other. There seems to be another problem here. It seems to us that a civil war is waged most often by civilians, as the name itself says, especially at the beginning of such a conflict. However, the Geneva Conventions are in conflict with this fact. All these problems, like many others, have not been taken into account by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber did not take into account our standpoint that in the case of persecution, the actus reus may be aimed against an individual, but the mens rea, especially as an element of widespread discrimination, has to be aimed against a group. This means that the attitude of the perpetrator to the group as a whole has to be evaluated. To say there was discrimination on political rather than racial or religious grounds would not only be more correct and true but would also contribute better to the reconciliation of the peoples on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Religious and ethnic differences remain, but the political division into those who are in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia and those who wanted to separate from it has been politically transcended. Yugoslavia no longer exists. There can no longer be any discrimination on this basis, but there can be on religious -- on a religious or ethnic basis. Acknowledging that the real reason of discrimination was political will calm down ethnic and religious passions, while attributing discrimination to ethnic and religious affiliation will only fan the flames further. The next ground of appeal, number 43, relates both to erroneous evaluation of certain mitigating circumstances and to a failure to take such circumstances into consideration. Thus, for example, inadequate attention was paid to the fact that Zigic, at the time of the commission of all the offences he has been charged with, was seriously injured and that it was then that his finger was amputated, for which reason he spent a certain period of time in hospital and is still an invalid today. This injury had serious psychological and physical consequences. Great pain and the loss of his index finger created in him a negative psychological state, but also they made it impossible for him to use this hand, especially to beat up other people. Finally, large bandages on his hand were a conspicuous identifying characteristic. In paragraph 746 of the judgement, his surrender to the Tribunal in April 1998 is not treated as a mitigating circumstance because he did this while he was in prison in Banja Luka for another crime. In the view of the Defence, this, without a doubt, is a mitigating circumstance, although maybe of less weight than had he surrendered while at large. In that period of time, nobody surrendered voluntarily, nor was Republika Srpska extraditing accused persons. It is enough to remember who was then in power in Republika Srpska. So there was no chance of him being extradited unless he wanted to surrender. No attention was paid to Zigic's admission to having perpetrated certain crimes and his public apology to the victims and expression of remorse. That this was important can be seen in the grounds of the judgement using this part of Zigic's statement in order to convict. When sentencing, the Trial Chamber also took account of the conviction for imprisonment in inhumane conditions as stated in paragraphs 764 and 766 of the judgement, while according to paragraphs 691 to 693 of the judgement, Zigic was not convicted of this offence. Finally, we shall illustrate the extent to which the positions on the length of the sentence of the Trial Chamber differ from the jurisprudence of this Tribunal by adducing an example starting from the fact that Zigic really did -- assuming, that is, that Zigic actually perpetrated everything that he has been convicted of. Zigic and Predrag Banovic, who was tried in case IT-02-65/S, according to what has been established so far, perpetrated practically the same crimes. They beat up people detained in camps and some people died of the beatings. The murder of one person, Drago Tokmadzic, and the beatings of two other prisoners is a common joint offence. However, Predrag Banovic committed five murders while Zigic committed four. Predrag Banovic committed 27 specific beatings and Zigic perpetrated almost three times less, that is ten, including cruel treatment of Hasan Karabasic. We feel that the responsibility of Banovic, who was a guard entrusted with the lives of these people is all the greater for that. Zigic, as has been said, surrendered; while Banovic, in order to evade responsibility before the Tribunal, fled to another country and hid there until he was caught and forcibly transferred here. Banovic entered into a plea agreement with the Prosecution which on this basis desisted from a further three murders he had been charged with. That is, there were a total of eight. Zigic did try to enter into a plea agreement with the Prosecution but only at the appeal stage because this was not possible with the previous Prosecution team. But he was not successful in this. It still has to be said that he confessed to some crimes and publicly expressed remorse, while Banovic, according to the Prosecution, did not display any substantial cooperation with the Prosecution. We feel that the facts relating to Banovic are well known at this Tribunal, and we adhere to the rule notoria non probatur. Now to refer to the standard of reasonable trier of fact. There is no doubt that anyone would say that Zigic deserved a lesser sentence than Banovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Going on to a new ground or a new phase of the argument? Would this be a convenient time do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I will continue where we stopped. I have been trying to be brief, but I do believe this is very tiring for you. I think I have a little time left, and I will certainly finish before the end of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When you return, it would help me in particular if you would advert to the last sentence of paragraph 746, which gives a reason why the Trial Chamber did not consider the fact of surrender to be a mitigating circumstance. It explained there, it said "Due to the fact that Zigic was imprisoned in Banja Luka at the time he surrendered to the Tribunal, the Tribunal does not consider his surrender to be a mitigating factor." That's just for you to reflect on and come back and to assist us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We will now suspend for 30 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The sitting is resumed. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If you permit me, first I would like to respond to your question which I have considered in the meantime. Mr. Zigic has given me the information that even on the official list of the Tribunal, he is being considered a person who voluntarily surrendered. In our appellant brief argument, paragraphs 421 to 422, we provided a more detailed explanation on this matter and the opinion of the Trial Chamber and gave a comment why we believe that this is a mitigating circumstance. I would like to read those two paragraphs if you permit us. The text is in English. I hope that the interpreters will not take it ill. [Previous translation continued]... [In English] It is stated: "That he was known by policemen of the Omarska Police Station as a petty criminal. However, this conclusion has no grounds at all, particularly since Zigic never had anything to do with the Omarska Police Station." In the same paragraph it is stated that: "The fact that Zigic surrendered to the Tribunal while he was in prison in Banja Luka, the Trial Chamber does not consider as a mitigating factor. The Defence is of the opinion that here the Trial Chamber erred. At that time, the authorities in the Republika Srpska in which, for instance, Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic held high positions would most certainly have not extradited Zigic to the Tribunal without his request. Besides, his conviction in the Republika Srpska was not effective yet, so his stay in prison was still considered as detention. He might also have expected withdrawal of the indictment raised against him by the Tribunal. At about the same time, charges against 14 persons were actually dropped, and he was among those mentioned in the same indictment. All the above shows that his surrender must be of significance as a mitigating factor, maybe not of the level it would have had if in fact he had been at large, but of significance it has to be. In any case, if the issue of surrender is viewed from the aspect of making it easier for the Tribunal to commence trials according to its indictments, then Zigic's surrender has the same significance as surrender of free persons." [Interpretation] This is what we stated in our appeal. Unfortunately, we've had to cut short a lot of that in our submissions today, and if you permit me, I would like to continue. Just to remind you, we stopped at a comparison of the Banovic and Zigic convictions where we previously said that Zigic was convicted for four and Banovic for five killings and Zigic for 10 and Banovic for 27 beatings. And we indicated a series of circumstances which could have a bearing on this matter. Then we recalled the standard of a reasonable trier of fact. There is no doubt that Zigic should be given a less severe sentence than Banovic. Of course I agree with that in the context of all the circumstances. But something has happened which cannot be justified by any arguments or plea bargains. Zigic was given a three times more severe sentence than Banovic. Banovic, for all of this, was sentenced to eight years' imprisonment while Zigic, for a lesser number of the same type of acts, was sentenced to 25 years. We believe that such a ratio not only harms the individuals who are being tried but it also subverts the authority of the Tribunal. The next ground of appeal is number 46 which relates to the claim that the Trial Chamber was biased. We admit that here we indicate the least popular grounds in any case to appeal a judgement. A good argument is required for such an assertion. I believe that through our previous submissions, we already provided several examples which address this matter. We mentioned that practically all the convictions were made while fully ignoring the Defence. When we say "ignore," it means that they were not mentioned nor was it indicated in any way that the submissions of the Defence were weighed and taken into account. Of course the Chamber is not obliged to mention every single piece of evidence, but it cannot simply fail to mention about ten eyewitnesses and then base its decision on speculation with a couple of items of circumstantial or hearsay evidence. In the case of the killing of Drago Tokmadzic, 11 witnesses were not mentioned while the conviction was based on contradictory and hearsay statements of the remaining two witnesses. We also mentioned examples with the witness Abdulah Brkic when the Defence was not permitted to question him about the killing of Becir Medunjanin at the time when the witness said that he was familiar with this incident. There is also the example with the questioning of the Witness T and his recognition of Zigic in the courtroom. We said that all of the Defence evidence was ignored in other cases as well. Exceptionally, they were weighed and assessed only in those small parts where these statements led to convictions. But how, then, can witnesses be believed in 1 or 2 per cent of their statement if they're not believed in everything else? An indicative example here is also Defence Witness DD10. The witness was invited to respond to the question of whether Zigic participated in the killing of Medunjanin and the witness categorically stated that he did not. However, the witness is mentioned in the judgement only when it was necessary to establish the responsibility of almost all of the accused, and in particular, Zigic. The witness is mentioned as proof that Medunjanin was beaten, then that Medunjanin succumbed to the beating, and the evidence charges Zigic for this. But the only thing that is not mentioned is the categoric statement of the witness that Zigic did not take part in this at all. Even in the event of acquittal, the Defence was fully ignored. So when we're talking about the decision regarding the charges for the massacre in Keraterm which took place on the 24th of July, 1992, all seven eyewitnesses of the Defence were ignored while the remaining three, who were alibi witnesses for Zigic, were said that they were not believable. That is why we are convinced that the Appeals Chamber here has quite a specific case in its to-date practice. The jurisprudence and especially the case law of the Tribunal were used quite selectively while, for example, the case law from the Celebici case is extensively used for the purposes of conviction. Opinions from the same case to which the Defence pointed were totally left out. The Trial Chamber did not even dwell on that. Finally, grounds of appeal number 47 in which it is generally stated that it refers to all other grounds defined in the appellant's brief but not mentioned here in this submission. This is something that can be objected to, indeed, which is exactly what the Prosecution does in claiming that it seems a little bit vague. But our appellant's brief is a total of 130 pages long. So what can we then say about charges encompassing all killings and all beatings in Omarska? We cannot find out everything about that, not even from at least half a million pages, which is what our case file runs to, including all the disclosed material. And to conclude, our submissions today constitute just a minor part of what we have stated in our appellant's brief and in our reply to the Prosecution's response. We have tried to base our submissions always on evidence and sound arguments. And finally, please allow me to say in spite of all these serious qualifications, once again to say and to express my personal great satisfaction for my participation in this large, complex, strenuous and responsible case before the Trial Chamber and also before this Appeals Chamber. This is an invaluable experience for me, and in spite of all the difficult moments, it has been one of the highlights of my profession and my career to date. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic, for your very helpful submissions. I turn to my colleagues on the Bench. There are no questions, Mr. Stojanovic. That does not indicate by any means a lack of interest in what you have said. Thank you very much. So now the next thing - and I congratulate you, particularly for finishing before the scheduled time - I would turn to the Prosecution. We still have some time. I don't know whether the Prosecution is in the position to commence its arguments now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, regrettably we were caught out, in fact, by the really precipitous, if I may say so, ending of my learned colleague's submission. In these circumstances we are not in a position to finish today but I can assure you in fact that we will be assiduous and as prompt in our submissions tomorrow, if it is allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's only an inquiry made out of curiosity because you are scheduled to begin tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed. Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then, we will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
